author: Kerry Smith
title: Oxfam: Israel has turned Gaza into a ‘toxic wasteland’
content:
Oxfam, in collaboration with the British-based Conflict and Environment Observatory, has published a new report on how Israel’s war on Gaza has made the air, soil and water dangerous to Palestinians now and for decades to come.

It found indicators of toxic contamination across almost the entire Gaza Strip.

Researchers used satellite-derived data, remote sensing analysis and geolocated conflict incident databases, to map contamination risks across Gaza. They drew on scientific and legal literature to assess exposure pathways and potential health consequences, and looked at the legal implications of environmental harm.

Their research found that that the scale and intensity of the Israeli military’s onslaught has affected approximately 78% of Gaza’s land area; the report’s spatial analysis identified indicators of potential contamination across more than 99% of the territory.

The report highlights the scale — a near-total geographical spread of pollution risks.

“Explosions and fires, together with the destruction and burning of buildings and infrastructure, have released airborne contaminants that settle onto rubble, soils and other surfaces, and are repeatedly resuspended by wind, vehicle movement and clearance of damaged buildings and debris,” the report said.

author: Kerry Smith
title: NT Environment Centre demands full federal assessment of gas pipeline
content:
The Environment Centre Northern Territory (ECNT) is calling on Murray Watt, the federal Environment and Water Minister, to undertake a full environmental impact statement of the APA Group’s fracked gas export pipeline.

The Queensland portion of the pipeline, 899 kilometres, was referred to Watt on November 26.

Rather than submit the full plan, the APA Group is referring small sections of its pipeline at a time in a bid to avoid environmental scrutiny.

The Environment Centre NT’s Acting CEO Bree Ahrens described this as “approval by stealth”.

The 1561-kilometre North to East Australia Pipeline (NEAP) to Gladstone’s export port in Queensland is one piece of a bigger network being built to move fracked gas from the Northern Territory to the east coast.

APA has even split the Bulloo Interlink Pipeline Project into two federal referrals — one for Queensland and one for NSW.

ECNT estimates the pipeline would enable major expansion of fracking in the NT, having the capacity to transport gas fracked from 1000 yet-to-be-approved gas wells.

Environment Centre NT CEO Bree Ahrens said the reason APA is splitting this approval process up is an attempt to “downplay the impact of this fracked gas export pipeline, and try and push through approvals without appropriate environmental scrutiny”.

author: Jeremy Brecher, Alexandria Shaner
title: United States: ‘Now the real work begins’
content:
Voters have just delivered an overwhelming rejection of United States President Donald Trump, opening a real opportunity to limit his drive to lock the country further into oil, gas and coal.

Labour historian and organiser, Jeremy Brecher, argues that this is only a starting point. Even if the worst of Trump’s fossil fuel agenda is blocked, the US is still on course to become a “fossil fuel island”, paying more for energy and falling behind economically while much of the world shifts to cheap solar, wind and batteries.

In his new report, The Greentech Revolution, Brecher makes the case that avoiding that fate means embracing a just transition to a fossil free economy.

Brecher stresses that cheaper technology won’t get us there on its own. What decides the outcome is who owns and controls the energy system, what it’s for, and whether ordinary people get a say. That fight is already underway in city halls, statehouses, and neighbourhoods organising against data centres.

With the midterms behind us, the real work begins now. I asked Brecher what that work looks like, from policy fights to organising well beyond the ballot box.

The midterms are over, and you say limiting Trump won’t be enough. What’s the gap between blocking the worst and actually building the alternative? Who has to close it, and where, outside of Congress?

We are already experiencing climate catastrophe and if we stay on our current trajectory it will only get worse and worse. We are already experiencing historic inequality, and if we stay on our current trajectory it will only get worse and worse. The same is true for our health, education, housing and all the other necessities of life.

Even if we block new Trump depredations, we will face an American era similar to Russia’s “Yeltsin Era” following the fall of the Soviet Union, when the legal, educational, healthcare, manufacturing and other basic systems went into unending decline — marked, for example, by a six-year drop in male life expectancy.

To change that will take the kind of transformative reconstruction that was envisioned by the Green New Deal. But because conditions have changed and deteriorated so much, we need to update that to what I call a “Green New Deal 2.0”.

From the beginning, the Green New Deal was a convergence of progressives inside the political system and social movements based in civil society.

The defeat of Trumpism in the 2026 midterm elections was similarly a convergence of outside-the-system forces like the No Kings coalition and inside-the-system Democrats who cared about Gaza, war, climate, the Constitution and the wellbeing of ordinary people. Plus, the decision by ordinary people that they had to step forward, whether it was by protecting their immigrant neighbours against ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] or in voting en masse against Republicans. Those same forces need to take the lead in developing the alternative — the “Green New Deal 2.0”.

The report argues the technology is already cheaper and winning. So why isn’t the US just switching? Who is holding it back, and what does the “fossil fuel island” cost ordinary people?

While the rest of the world is racing to switch to fossil-free greentech energy production and consumption, the US is going in the opposite direction. This is due to two main factors.

The first is the power of the fossil fuel industry.

Even under Joe Biden’s “Build Back Better” program, supposedly “green” policies like carbon capture and hydrogen were coined into profits for fossil fuel developers while the US underwent its largest ever expansion of natural gas.

The second is a nationalist drive to use energy policy for geopolitical power.

The Biden administration put high tariffs on cheap Chinese solar and EV imports that could have revolutionised American energy use. The Trump administration put both of these dynamics on steroids. It has tried to destroy Greentech energy initiatives not only in the US but worldwide. And it has provided vast subsidies for fossil fuel expansion.

But this is a fool’s strategy. You can see the actual results for ordinary Americans in the price of gasoline, heating oil, diesel fuel and electricity. And you can see the long-term effects of fossil fuel domination in the devastating heat waves, floods, wildfires and other products of climate change.

Your report says technology never dictates the form or speed of social change. Why does that matter right now? The “free lunch” idea is easy to read as “the market will handle it”. What does it mean in your argument, and what doesn’t it mean?

Converting to “green energy” used to be seen as a burdensome, if necessary, cost of creating a climate-safe economy. But the Greentech revolution has reduced the cost of producing and using fossil-free energy so much that the “green transition” is now not an expense but a “free lunch”. But who is going to get to enjoy that lunch?

As we see with the hyperscale datacentre buildout, massive investment in solar and wind energy can simply be a way to increase profits for a few hyperscalers, while generating environmental destruction and higher energy bills for the rest of us. A Green New Deal 2.0 can become a vehicle for the massive opposition to data centres and destructive forms of energy development, even as the Elon Musks of the world use “green energy” to pursue their nefarious ends.

You write that the transition isn’t just swapping energy sources. It also means asking what gets produced, at what scale, for whose benefit, and under whose control. What would answering that look like in practice? Ann Arbor’s public Sustainable Energy Utility and Seattle’s community assemblies seem like early examples.

In my book The Green New Deal from Below, in my “Greentech Revolution” report, and in my current series of commentaries on the “Green New Deal 2.0”, I describe scores of examples of fossil free energy initiatives in communities, cities, and states around the country, including the Ann Arbor and Seattle examples you mention.

Part of what is important here is the creativity of these initiatives, the way they develop multiple new approaches that replace fossil fuel extraction and burning while meeting the pressing needs of their communities.

With the raft of more progressive city and state governments installed by the 2026 midterm elections, there is a great opportunity for such initiatives. They can show that the Green New Deal 2.0 is not just a pipe dream, let alone a threat to working people’s living standards, but a practical, achievable means to make our lives — and our climate — better and more affordable.

Fossil fuels and renewables are both growing right now. Why isn’t adding Greentech enough, and what does it take to actually shrink fossil fuel extraction and burning? How do “leave it in the ground” fights fit in?

Until fossil fuel extraction and burning are halted, the effects of global warming, already devastating, will continue to intensify. Adding more green energy won’t forestall more apocalyptic floods, fires, heatwaves and superstorms, unless it is combined with a rapid phasing out of fossil fuels.

“All the above” policies that promote both fossil fueled and fossil free energy just accelerate global warming and its consequences.

Hundreds of local campaigns against coal-fired power plants and fossil fuel pipelines have exposed the climate crisis, reduced significant amounts of greenhouse gas emissions, and shown that people are not powerless to affect climate destruction. Such actions are not only effective in themselves; they also lay the groundwork for insistence on government policies to halt fossil fuel extraction and burning.

The data centre rebellion is one of the more surprising stories in the report. What does it tell us about organising outside electoral channels? Does it point toward democratic control over major infrastructure decisions, as opposed to deciding by corporate investment plans?

As a historian of social movements, I find the “data centre rebellion” embodies the often disregarded capacity of ordinary people to organise themselves — and the unexpected ways their action can affect governments, corporations and other institutions.

The data centre rebellion is overwhelmingly centered in working-class communities. While it has received help from various quarters, its core is the self-organisation of urban and rural residents to fight a direct threat.

Dissolving divisions between red and blue constituencies, it has highlighted the question of whether a few billionaires should have the power to disrupt the lives of ordinary people. It has passed anti-datacentre laws in hundreds of jurisdictions. And it made a significant contribution to the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections.

Whether it can parlay its successes into fuller control of corporate decision-making now hangs in the balance.

If you could pick a few policy fights to win in the next year, which would they be, and what can’t be left to policy at all?

Stop Green New Deal “hushing” — the silencing or even trashing of Green New Deal advocacy in response to Trump’s denigration.

Instead, articulate a transformative vision of a Green New Deal 2.0 based on greentech energy combined with affordability, jobs and justice.

Start implementing that vision immediately in states, cities and communities, drawing on the scores of Green New Deal from Below initiatives already under way in communities, cities and states.

Promote a convergence of the Green New Deal 2.0 and the data centre rebellion. Focus on the need for democratic control of corporations and their technologies, and on the harmful energy and environmental effects of data centres.

[Reprinted from ZNetwork.org and The Labor Network for Sustainability. View or download the full report here. Jeremy Brecher is a co-founder of the Labor Network for Sustainability and is active in peace, labour, environmental and other social movements. He wrote Strike! and Global Village or Global Pillage and is an award-winning documentary maker. Alexandria Shaner is an editor of ZNetwork.org, a writer for Extinction Rebellion, and is active with the Democratic Socialists of America and Food Not Bombs.]

author: Peter Boyle
title: Capitalism hijacks another climate summit
content:
Given the heatwaves in Europe, the catastrophic floods in Nepal and wildfire crisis in Indonesia, you would hope that the recent COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkiye, would have reached agreement on stronger action to deal with the global climate emergency.

But COP31 totally failed to take the urgently-needed action. According to some assessments, it might have even set back the snail’s pace progress towards the non-binding targets set under the 2015 Paris Agreement, which had its goal to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

“Governments had a chance to show that international cooperation can still deliver for people," said Climate Action Network International (CAN) in a press release on November 22. "Instead, the world’s wealthiest countries spent two weeks dismantling the very commitments that offered some hope of protection.”

With the exception of 2009 (in Copenhagen), every COP summit since 2003 has led to a loose and non-binding formal agreement.

Turkiye’s co-host Australia, one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters, led the negotiations for the draft Antalya Accords.

The draft conceded a failure to keep the global temperature from rising 1.5˚C above the pre-industrial revolution level, but the root cause of this — fossil fuels — was not even mentioned in the agreement.

The European Union, Panama and many vulnerable island nations refused to agree to any text that did not explicitly address them.

This disagreement ultimately prevented the summit from reaching consensus, said the team of climate experts from University College London (UCL) attending COP31.

“This has been the modus operandi of these summits — they start with a more ambitious draft text that gets weakened as it comes closer to adoption … But removing fossil fuels from a climate text is like removing mention of cigarettes in an anti-smoking campaign — it was simply too much for many countries to accept.”

While the UCL team labelled this outcome a “victory for fossil fuel producing nations”, CAN pointed out that the European Union exploited the legitimate outrage by the most vulnerable states from the Global South to advance its own agenda.

“Much of the attention on COP31 has focused on the disappearance of fossil fuel language from the cover decision. But that story has helped hide the obstruction taking place across the negotiations. With the United States absent, the EU has stepped into the role of chief obstructor, while presenting itself as a champion of climate ambition — even going so far as to position itself as the first to reject the cover decision in the closing plenary.

“The EU and other developed countries spent two weeks blocking progress even on existing commitments. The EU refused to engage on a baseline for tripling adaptation finance and obstructed efforts to clarify developed countries’ obligations to provide public finance under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement.

“Developed countries demanded that developing countries move faster away from fossil fuels while denying them the resources to do it. Some developed countries dressed up existing policies as ambitious fossil fuel transition road maps, even as they continued to expand fossil fuel production at home. Having blocked the means to achieve a Just Transition, they then tried to pin the failure of COP31 on developing countries.”

While the major fossil fuel exporting states, like Australia and Saudi Arabia, are culpable, ultimately it was capitalism and the world’s richest states that hijacked COP31 and previous COP meetings.

They turned this climate summit into a trade fare for fossil fuel companies, carbon dioxide removal promoters and the AI industry, which descended on Antalya in large numbers to justify the ongoing use of fossil fuels.

“COPs have become greenwashed circuses. That is the reality,” activist Greta Thunberg said at COP31. “Of course it is absolutely crucial that we still do everything we possibly can because this is an opportunity to mobilise people … The climate disasters that we have seen recently [are] something that scientists and people living on the front lines have been warning about for decades.

“And we also need to acknowledge that the COPs are not sufficient to prevent a climate catastrophe.”

Future COP summits will also fail if we don’t succeed in building the strong people-power movements that are needed for real change, which as Green Left has argued since it formed in 1991, requires system change.

Capitalism has to be replaced by a system that puts people and planet before profit.

You can help build the movement for system change by becoming a Green Left supporter or donating to our 2026 Fighting Fund.

Climate Action Network International

author: Susan Price
title: People’s Climate Summit at COP31: ‘Defend life, rebuild the world!’
content:
As Marxist economist Michael Roberts reported, the United Nations Climate Change Conference 2026 (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, was labeled by climate activists as the “worst COP ever” as delegates divided over the wording of the summit’s final communiqué.

All mention of the need to phase out fossil fuels had, by then, been removed and it fell way short on the climate financing needed for developing nations to deal with climate adaptation and mitigation.

Critics slammed its emphasis on the as-yet untested carbon capture and storage technology as an incentive for the continued investment in fossil fuels and associated infrastructure.

The draft also projected that the world would overshoot 1.5⁰C of global warming.

As Peter Boyle argues in this week’s Green Left: “While the major fossil fuel exporting states, like Australia and Saudi Arabia, are culpable, ultimately it was capitalism and the world’s richest states that hijacked COP31” turning it “into a trade fare for fossil fuel companies, carbon dioxide removal promoters and the AI industry, which descended on Antalya in large numbers to justify the ongoing use of fossil fuels.”

Meanwhile, ecological activists, indigenous peoples and civil society groups came together for a counter People’s Climate Summit in Antalya, from November 14–18. It was organised by three major umbrella organisations of the ecology movement in Türkiye — the Climate Justice Coalition, the Ecology Union and the Environmental Platform of Türkiye.

The summit opened with a march for climate justice, in which thousands participated.

There are restrictions on organising protests in Turkey, with ecological activists reportedly treated as though they are terrorists. Several environmental activists were arrested in the lead up to COP31. In spite of these threats, about 500 people took part in the counter summit, which was assisted by the organisers of the previous People Climate Summit in Belem, Brazil.

Protesters, such as Malaysian climate activist Amalen Sathananthar, also took their protest inside the “blue zone”, interrupting a speech by Murat Kurum, Turkey’s COP president.

As the Guardian reported, “Sathananthar, a member of the Artivist Network, stood on a table holding a noose of red rope around his neck and wearing a T-shirt with the message ‘You are killing the future’ painted on it.

“‘You are killing the future,’ he shouted. ‘Why don’t you just kill me now. The climate crisis is killing us, and you do nothing. You don’t remove fossil fuels, you are killing 1.5C.”

Ahead of the counter summit, Co-Chair of the Pro-Kurdish DEM Parti Tülay Hatimoğulları told the media that states, corporations and civil society groups that support them have “turned COP31 into a pretext to perpetuate a system that is driving the world into darkness and threatening the lives of all living beings”.

The People’s Climate Summit’s adopted a declaration, Defending Life, Rebuilding the World. It slammed the COP’s acceptance of a 1.5⁰C overshoot and demanded that to keep the Earth’s climate stable a safe ecological limit must be 350 parts per million of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

“Even holding global warming at 1.5°C will have irreversible ecological consequences. It is unacceptable to defer the target to a time when those making the decisions will no longer be alive and to make warming above 1.5°C the new normal for this century,” the declaration said.

“Every increment of warming deepens the destruction and increases irreversible losses. Emissions reduction targets must therefore be revised to meet the needs of nature and peoples, rather than corporate interests. We must insist on avoiding an overshoot and on progressively bringing warming below 1.5°C.”

The declaration highlighted that the climate crisis deepens preexisting inequalities. It rejected “policies that profit from disasters, turn devastation into new opportunities for capital accumulation and use emergencies to entrench exceptional forms of rule and curtail social rights”.

Pointing the blame directly at the economic and political system, the document said: “The climate crisis cannot be understood apart from a capitalist mode of production, that treats nature as something to be used without limit, and human labour as an input whose cost must continually be driven down. The drive to keep accumulating capital is increasingly at odds with the planet’s ecological limits and with what people need to live in dignity.”

Responding to the growth in Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure, the declaration said the rapid expansion of data centres “could become one of the defining ecological problems of our time”, due to their demand for electricity, fresh water, minerals and other raw materials.

“We must therefore ask not only how data centres are powered, but also who decides what they are for, at what scale they are built and who bears the ecological cost.”

In terms of false solutions, including nuclear power, carbon trading and carbon capture and storage, the declaration said: “We do not see the climate crisis as a technical problem that can be solved simply by replacing fossil fuels with other energy sources or putting a price on carbon emissions. The crisis raises questions about what production is for, how resources are distributed, who makes decisions and whose needs shape the way society is organised.”

The counter summit adopted a raft of demands, including that ecocide “be recognised as a crime under national and international law”; that indigenous peoples’ right to free, prior and informed consent be recognised; and that “the criminalisation and repression of those resisting ecological destruction” end.

The summit also criticised so-called “green transitions” that are damaging ecologies and “deepening unequal trade relations, especially in the Global South”, saying “One region’s energy transition cannot come at the cost of another’s destruction”.

It called for the rapid, fair and binding phase out of fossil fuels, and for climate finance to consist of public grants not loans, which are adequate, accessible and free of new debt.

It called for a just transition, for the public ownership of energy production and for the distribution to be placed under the democratic planning of workers and communities.

Declaring that “war and militarism are inseparable from the climate crisis”, the summit condemned Israel’s genocide in Gaza, occupation and forced displacement of Palestinians. It demanded “an immediate and permanent end to the violence, an end to the occupation, accountability for those responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity, and recognition of the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination”.

It also demanded that “[t]he harm caused by conflict over the Kurdish question to the living and non-living constituents of nature … be fully documented and the findings made public” and said that “peace begins when the guns fall silent and endures when human and other-than-human life can flourish.”

The declaration affirmed that ensuring food sovereignty “requires collective control over land, water, seeds and the means of production, and protection of the rights of peasants, farmworkers, fishers, pastoralists and local communities” and that agroecology “be recognised as a central approach to climate adaptation in agriculture and food systems” and publicly funded.

“The capitalist order, savage capitalism, is consumed by the pursuit of unlimited growth and maximising its profits at an ever-increasing pace; far from abandoning the plunder of nature, it is deepening it,” said Hatimoğullar.

However, she said, the polluters of the world are “not as mighty as they are thought to be. Those who built this system of capitalist brutality, are not as powerful as we assume.

“As long as we, all the peoples of the world, workers, labourers, women, young people, nature and human rights defenders unite our struggles, lock arms and succeed in marching with a shared perspective, we can change this order. We will change this order. We will certainly succeed.”

author: Sonny Melencio
title: Pax Silica: Who benefits, whose industrial strategy? A rejoinder to supporters of Pax Silica
content:
Proponents of Pax Silica promise factories, exports, and skilled jobs. We’ve heard those promises before.

After decades of building export zones and selling electronics abroad, Philippine semiconductor production remains concentrated in assembly, testing and packaging.

Under the terms being offered, Pax Silica will deepen this pattern and further stunt Philippine industrialisation. The government is committing public land, infrastructure and worker training to a foreign-led supply chain without securing the commitments needed to build our own industrial capacity.

The US State Department launched Pax Silica in December 2025 to secure supply chains critical to Washington’s rivalry with China. The founding group included the United States, Israel, Australia, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Britain. They came to the table with industrial, financial, or technological advantages of their own.

By November 16, the declaration reportedly had 26 signatories, with Singapore and the Philippines reported as the only ASEAN members among them.

The Philippines joined after Washington had set the initiative’s priorities. In an April 9 letter to US Under Secretary of State Jacob Helberg, Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) President Joshua Bingcang proposed a Pax Silica coordination hub in a 4000-acre [1619 hectare] economic security zone in New Clark City, Tarlac.

To sweeten the offer, the BCDA proposed a two-year rent-free period as the Philippine government’s contribution.

Washington has clear economic, geopolitical and military interests in the initiative. It wants reliable access to critical minerals, advanced chips, computing power and data infrastructure. It wants to organise those supply chains around the United States and its partners in its rivalry with China.

Advanced computing serves both civilian and military purposes, and Washington is pursuing Pax Silica alongside its broader military alliance strategy in the Indo-Pacific.

That broader strategy was on display on November 4 in Cebu. On the sidelines of the ASEAN defense ministers’ meeting, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and his counterparts from the Philippines, Japan and Australia met under the informal grouping known as the “Squad”.

They agreed on a Manila-based coordination centre to align defense investments, intelligence sharing and military deterrence against China.

The Philippines enters this arrangement without a geostrategy of its own. The Philippine Development Plan 2023–2028 gives the state an active role in building infrastructure, training workers and supporting selected industries.

Yet it relies on the neoliberal framework of private investment, public-private partnerships and integration into global supply chains. That leaves investors with considerable power over what gets built and who captures the gains.

This is how dependent capitalism works. Decisions about financing, technology and production are often made abroad.

At home, Philippine oligarchs earn substantial returns from land, property and concessions. For them, building factories, engineering teams and supplier networks takes years of investment with less certain returns.

The semiconductor industry shows where the leverage lies. US-based NVIDIA dominates the market for AI accelerators. Taiwan’s TSMC leads in advanced chip fabrication. The Netherlands’ ASML is the sole commercial supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography systems. Each controls a capability that takes years and enormous investment to build.

Their governments use these points of leverage to restrict China’s access to advanced technology.

The 2023 agreement among the United States, the Netherlands and Japan covered certain chip-making equipment. Dutch licensing rules restrict exports of advanced ASML machines, while US export controls separately affect certain NVIDIA chip sales and TSMC shipments to China.

The Philippines is offering to host a semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing hub in Tarlac that would serve this supply chain.

The question is what capabilities the country would gain. Building the engineering teams, research institutions, and supplier networks that would give us greater control over what we produce requires an industrial strategy of our own.

Successive Philippine governments have treated access to foreign markets and capital as a substitute for building domestic productive capacity.

Years back before Philippine independence, the 1946 Bell Trade Act shaped postwar economic relations, including through an arrangement that gave Americans parity rights in exploiting Philippine natural resources and operating public utilities. The Laurel–Langley Agreement later revised those trade terms. A separate military bases agreement entrenched US military access.

Under Fidel V Ramos, entry into the World Trade Organization was sold as a route to greater competitiveness. Import competition intensified while many Filipino farmers and producers still lacked affordable credit, irrigation, storage and processing facilities.

Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo’s promise of food on every table carried forward the same faith in liberalisation. Opening markets did little to fill the gaps successive governments had left in agriculture and industry.

Our export zones offer the clearest test of what Pax Silica promises.

Since the creation of the Bataan Export Processing Zone in Mariveles, these zones have brought few factories, jobs, exports, and technical skills. Yet semiconductor production still centers on assembly, testing and packaging, with limited chip design and no major commercial wafer fabrication.

The head of the Semiconductor and Electronics Industries in the Philippines (SEIPI) has argued that wafer fabrication is important to the industry’s long-term competitiveness and has identified shortages of specialised workers, local suppliers, and a proven production base as barriers to attracting a major plant.

The World Bank estimates that foreign value added accounts for roughly half the gross export value of Philippine computer and electronics manufacturing. That helps explain how billions in electronics exports can coexist with a thin local supplier base.

Meanwhile, manufacturing’s share of GDP fell from roughly a quarter in 2001 to around a sixth in 2024. Several forces drove that decline, and decades of expanding economic zones failed to reverse it.

Under the proposal, the government supplies land, infrastructure, and incentives. Foreign firms can locate the operations that suit their supply chains here while keeping control of the technology and the most profitable stages of production elsewhere.

Domestic conglomerates can earn from property and concessions even if Philippine industry gains little productive capacity.

Every public peso and hectare committed on those terms is a resource we could use to develop local producers and meet domestic needs. That is how a project can add factories and still stunt industrialisation.

The costs also fall unevenly. If the conversion of thousands of acres displaces farmers or encroaches on Indigenous ancestral lands, who bears the loss? The people whose land and livelihoods are at stake must have the right to decide what happens in their communities. Their rights must carry more weight than the government’s bid to attract investors.

A large AI data center is a plausible component, given the country’s limited computing infrastructure at that scale. If it goes ahead, the government must show who will control the computing capacity, which Philippine industries will be able to use it, and who will bear the cost of the electricity and water it requires considering that all these were privatized to firms out to earn more profits and pass on the costs to consumers.

Supporters who dismiss socialist and progressive critics as ideological should defend their own premise.

After decades of liberalisation and investor incentives, what grounds do they have for claiming that another foreign-led economic zone will build the industries the country needs?

The burden is on the Marcos Jr. administration to show who will own the technology, which Filipino industries will grow, and what the country will retain after the incentives expire.

The Philippines needs an industrial strategy anchored in public investment, domestic production and the needs of workers, farmers and communities.

That means building local supplier networks, funding public research and engineering, and tying public support for investors to enforceable commitments to develop Philippine capabilities.

Washington is using Pax Silica to consolidate its lead in AI and shape the supply chains that sustain it. The Marcos Jnr administration is offering our land, minerals and labour to carry out that strategy.

Our task is to build an industrial strategy of our own. Not through the dynasties, oligarchs and their neoliberal cohorts.

[Sonny Melencio is the chairperson of the Partido Lakas Ng Masa (Party of the Labouring Masses).]

author: Rudi Hartono, Peter Boyle
title: ‘Rising authoritarianism and militarism’ in Indonesia under Prabowo
content:
As the Indonesian economy sinks deeper into crisis, President Prabowo Subianto's government is becoming more authoritarian. Peter Boyle spoke to Rudi Hartono, one of the founding editors of the progressive publication Merdika.id about the current political situation. Hartono, a former editor of Berdikari Online left the People’s Democratic Party (PRD) because it moved to the right.

Recent events in Indonesia — the deployment of thousands of soldiers and tanks in Jakarta following reports of electronic surveillance [wiretapping] targeting President Prabowo Subianto and other government officials and the police raid on Gadjah Mada University — are reminiscent of the Suharto dictatorship’s New Order regime. Is a new and dangerous situation developing? If so, what lies behind it?

Yes, we are witnessing clear symptoms of rising authoritarianism and militarism. Although many had predicted this trajectory since Prabowo’s election victory, the speed and intensity of the process have been striking.

Since June 2026, the military has once again been deployed to confront protests — a move that evokes memories of the New Order. Large-scale troop mobilisations occurred during the demonstrations on October 20 (marking two years of the Prabowo-Gibran administration) and October 28 (Youth Pledge Day).

On one of those days, I received a WhatsApp message containing a video of tanks and marching soldiers on the streets, accompanied by the caption: “Thank your friends [referring to former PRD members who now support Prabowo and hold positions in government] for bringing the military back onto the streets.”

Yet the presence of soldiers on the streets only completes the picture of authoritarian consolidation that has taken shape over the past two years under Prabowo-Gibran.

Today, the 1998 reformasi has become little more than an artifact. Political power is once again concentrated in the executive (the presidency).

Many of the president’s remarks in speeches have quickly turned into policy — such as the roof-tile standardisation program or foreign-language lessons. The House of Representatives (DPR) has been reduced to a chorus, much like under the New Order.

There is no genuine opposition in the DPR. Even the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle (PDIP), which remains outside the ruling coalition, has tended to be permissive toward the deteriorating situation.

The judiciary has suffered a similar fate: it is filled with government-aligned figures. The mechanisms of checks and balances have effectively disappeared.

It is not only the legislative and judicial branches that have been subdued. We are also seeing a process of recentralisation that is stripping regional and local governments of authority, fiscal resources, and responsibilities. Regional autonomy — one of the key achievements of the 1998 reform — is now little more than a skeleton being dragged toward its grave.

At the same time, freedom of expression is being heavily repressed. Paid "buzzers" [opinion-shapers] are deployed to drown out public criticism on social media, while the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs actively removes critical content. Cases of threats, intimidation, and doxxing against citizens in digital spaces are common. Mainstream media have adopted self-censorship. Under former President Joko Widowo (Jokowi), certain individuals monitored the media from the outside; under Prabowo, his people have entered the newsrooms themselves to supervise from within.

The presidential wiretapping issue, which provided the pretext for mobilising more than 20,000 troops and tanks on Jakarta’s streets, cannot be read simply as a clash between two elite factions. It more closely resembles the autogolpe [“self-coup”] schemes frequently seen in Latin America.

In my view, the issue was manufactured to serve three purposes at once. First, it supplied a justification for deploying more soldiers onto the streets. Second, it diverted public attention from structural problems — economic crisis, corruption, militarism, and others — toward a security narrative. Third, it was a crude tactic to redirect vertical public anger at the regime into a drama of elite infighting.

Before the wiretapping story surfaced, the regime was already under pressure from multiple fronts: forest fires in Kalimantan, Sumatra, and Papua; mass food poisoning from the free nutritious meal program (MBG) that has affected more than 50,000 children; the militarisation and expanding role of the armed forces across almost every civilian domain; corruption cases implicating senior officials, including Agrarian and Spatial Planning Minister Nusron Wahid and Customs Director General Djaka Budhi Utama (a former Kopassus colleague of Prabowo who was involved in the 1997–98 activist abductions); and widespread public criticism of priority programs such as the MBG and the Red-and-White Village Cooperatives (Kopdes Merah Putih), which absorb enormous budgets.

Prior to that issue, large-scale protests had already taken place in major cities including Jakarta, Yogyakarta, Surabaya, Malang, Semarang, Makassar, and others. These actions were driven primarily by young people — especially Generation Z — and the middle class. Demonstrators raised the three-finger salute, adopted from The Hunger Games, as a symbol of protest against a regime growing increasingly authoritarian.

Under Prabowo-Gibran there have already been more than ten large-scale protests. The driving force remains young people (particularly Gen Z) and the middle class. Notably, more and more mothers and young women are leading and shaping these actions. Public support has been substantial: many women have opened community kitchens for demonstrators. People from various walks of life — office workers, ride-hailing drivers, academics and influencers — have joined the protests.

The less encouraging news is that trade unions and the left have been almost invisible. At a time when democratic space is shrinking, economic conditions are deteriorating and the military is once again intervening in industrial disputes, one would expect unions to be the most alarmed. Instead, the opposite has occurred: the labour movement appears largely indifferent. Prabowo-Gibran’s success in coopting virtually all union elites, including those on the left, has helped isolate organised labour from the emerging protest movement.

How significant is the impact of tensions between factions within the government and Gibran Rakabuming Raka’s resignation as vice president?

Before Jokowi brought him into the cabinet as defense minister in 2019, Prabowo’s political prospects were essentially finished. He had run for president three times and lost each time. Before receiving Jokowi’s endorsement for the 2024 election, his electability stood below 30%. His chances of winning were slim. At that point, most of Jokowi’s supporters and the broader public regarded Ganjar Pranowo (the PDIP candidate) as the natural successor to Jokowi and his policies.

Prabowo understood that victory required Jokowi’s support. He successfully exploited the rift between Jokowi and PDIP. According to Tempo, Prabowo asked Jokowi as many as five times to put forward his son, Gibran Rakabuming, as running mate — and succeeded.

As a last-minute vice-presidential candidate, Gibran faced multiple problems, from age to competence. The Constitutional Court, then led by Jokowi’s brother-in-law, changed the rules to grant Gibran the necessary normative legitimacy. Questions about his diploma, which continue to be raised today, were part of the broader scenario by election organisers — including the General Elections Commission and the Election Supervisory Agency — to clear the path for his candidacy.

Gibran’s nomination cannot be viewed in isolation. It must be seen as part of a wider struggle between the interests of Jokowi and Prabowo, who employed various means — including measures that damaged the principles of free and fair elections — to secure a Prabowo-Gibran victory.

With Jokowi’s backing — which included mobilising state apparatus and resources, including social-assistance programs for the poor (a form of pork-barrel politics) — Prabowo-Gibran won. The police general recently arrested in connection with the wiretapping case was among those who had helped deploy security forces to secure that victory.

Today that alliance has broken apart. This is nothing new in Indonesian politics. Elite or party coalitions in Indonesia are rarely built on shared political programs or ideological proximity; they rest on mutual interests in accessing public office and state resources. Since the New Order, capital accumulation in Indonesia has been built on close ties between the bureaucracy, political elites, and business groups.

Access to power means access to state projects, concessions, business permits, natural resources, credit, and various economic privileges. Indonesia’s economic engine still rests heavily on the extractive sector. Most of the country’s wealthy are linked to extractive industries, which in turn are intertwined with alliances between businesspeople, officials and the military.

The Prabowo-Jokowi split must therefore be understood in political-economic terms. Under Jokowi, policy was relatively accommodating to business and the full spectrum of oligarchic interests. Under Prabowo, with its command-style economy and recentralisation, capital accumulation is being redirected primarily toward the president’s family and cronies. Hashim Djojohadikusumo, Prabowo’s younger brother, now holds 26 concurrent positions and controls numerous projects, particularly in oil, gas and bioenergy.

For civil society, the Prabowo-Jokowi rupture is little more than a clash of interests between oligarchic factions. Both sides are problematic.

At the grassroots level, however — especially among those who once admired Jokowi for his infrastructure projects and social-assistance programs — the split has generated a new opposition bloc and broadened the spectrum of opposition.

The economy is deteriorating. What are the main trends and their causes?

On paper, the economic numbers look respectable. Growth remains above 5%. Inflation is kept below 3%. The budget deficit stays under the 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) threshold. Open unemployment stands at 7.4 million (4.7%).

Yet these figures mask the underlying reality. From the outset, the administration inherited an extremely narrow fiscal space — a combination of tax shortfalls, a weakening rupiah and debt pressures (both principal and interest). Prabowo has attempted to address the fiscal problem through efficiency measures. The problem is that his version of efficiency is highly selective. He has formed an oversized cabinet (nine ministers and 57 deputy ministers), created numerous new ministries and agencies with overlapping functions and authorities, and drawn criticism for frequent overseas trips with large entourages, as well as for state ceremonies and the far-from-simple lifestyles of officials.

Despite the constrained fiscal space, Prabowo has pushed ahead with populist programs such as the MBG and the Red-and-White Village Cooperatives. These initiatives triggered public protests from the beginning. Many people support continuing the programs but argue they should be better targeted — limited to children from poor families and stunting-prone areas — in order to conserve budget. The government has refused to listen.

To ease the fiscal squeeze, there has been discussion of abolishing the 3% deficit-to-GDP ceiling (derived from the 1992 Maastricht Treaty). The government is also pushing for greater concentration of assets and capital under state control. Examples include Danantara, a super-holding company that oversees the assets, capital and investments of all state-owned enterprises. Exports are now being channeled through a single door under Danantara. There is talk of workers’ severance funds being deposited with and managed by the government. Most recently, the newly passed Asset Confiscation Law channels seized funds to an agency under presidential control.

A second issue is debt pressure. On paper, Indonesia’s total debt stands at 40.3% of GDP — still well below the legal limit. The debt-to-GDP ratio, however, is largely irrelevant. Debts are not paid with GDP. The government services debt through revenue (taxes, non-tax receipts and grants) or new financing (fresh borrowing). Measured against state revenue, the ratio already exceeds 300%. In other words, it would take three years of state revenue to cover the debt. Interest payments alone absorb nearly 20% of state revenue — meaning that for every five rupiah of revenue, one rupiah is set aside for debt servicing.

A third problem is low tax revenue. The tax-to-GDP ratio in 2025 was only 9.31% — the lowest in ASEAN [the Association of South East Asian Nations] and the third-lowest in the Asia-Pacific region. Indonesia’s tax base remains narrow because the manufacturing sector has not developed adequately. The majority of Indonesian workers are in the informal sector, earning low wages with no job security or social protection. Even formal-sector wages average only about Rp 3.4 million per month.

Meanwhile, Indonesia is a highly unequal country. According to CELIOS’s 2026 economic inequality report, the wealth of Indonesia’s 50 richest people equals that of the 55 million poorest. The World Inequality Lab’s 2026 report notes that the top 10% of Indonesians hold 59.4% of national wealth, while the bottom 50% control only 2.5%.

Ironically, amid this wide inequality, the wealth of Indonesian officials has risen sharply. At least 11 officials possess wealth measured in the trillions of rupiah, including President Prabowo Subianto and five ministers. Nearly every minister holds assets in the billions.

Ironically, while Prabowo’s supporters claim he is a socialist, there has been not the slightest word or intention of introducing a wealth tax. Instead, problematic super-rich individuals have been protected through instruments such as Patriot Bonds and Merah-Putih Bonds.

A fourth issue is declining purchasing power. Almost every segment of society reports weaker buying power. Hard numbers are difficult to present because the government denies the problem. Observable phenomena include “downgrading” of consumption — switching to cheaper products, reducing portion sizes or shopping frequency, or cooking at home more often — along with the practices of “eating savings” and “eating debt.” The middle class has shrunk by roughly 10.6 million people in just six years. Businesses, especially micro-, small, and medium enterprises, complain of empty customers; many have closed.

Regional tensions are rising because of forest fires in Kalimantan and Sumatra. What are the impacts in Indonesia, and does this annual crisis reflect chronic corruption?

Indonesia experiences forest fires almost every year, but this year’s have been among the worst. According to Nusantara Atlas, nearly 2 million hectares of forest burned in Kalimantan, Sumatra and Papua. Some 41.1 million people were affected, of whom 401,586 suffered acute respiratory infections.

Bitterly, findings by Indonesian Forum for Living Environment (WALHI) and field reports show that many hotspots overlap with corporate concession areas, particularly those of forestry and oil-palm plantation companies. This has fueled widespread suspicion that the fires were deliberately set for land clearing. Videos have circulated showing oil-palm seedlings discovered at post-fire sites.

The fires reveal several things. First, they cannot be separated from the extractivist economic model — an economy based on large-scale, intensive exploitation of natural resources for export, whether in raw form or with minimal processing, to global markets.

This sector is intertwined with bribery, lobbying, rent-seeking and cronyism. Businesses are built on strong relationships or access to political power. The oligarchs surrounding President Prabowo have largely accumulated their wealth from extractive industries. The president himself has repeatedly expressed support for the expansion of the palm-oil sector.

Second, the government has appeared incompetent in handling the disaster. When the public demanded that the forest and land fires be declared a national disaster — which would have triggered the mobilisation of national resources and budgets — the government refused. The stated reason was budgetary. At the same time, the state spends approximately Rp 1.2 trillion a day on the free meal program. Many have asked why the country still lacks dedicated water-bombing aircraft when a Canadair CL-415 amphibious water bomber costs only about Rp 500 billion. Stopping the free meal program for a single day, they note, could fund two such planes.

Third, the government’s inability to manage successive local disasters — floods and landslides in Sumatra in late 2025, a two-day blackout across Sumatra in May, and this year’s forest fires — has fueled public dissatisfaction in the regions. In Aceh, that discontent has revived separatist sentiment. On social media, residents of various regions have begun raising the issue of federalism.

Of course, neither separatism nor federalism is necessarily the best solution, given that local political character and dynamics are often no better.

author: Stan Miller, Victor Osprey
title: France: ‘The leadership of the movement belongs to the students themselves’
content:
Stan Miller is a member of the French revolutionary socialist organisation Nouveau parti anticapitaliste — Révolutionnaires (New Anticapitalist Party — Revolutionary, NPA–R) in Montpellier. He spoke to Victor Osprey on November 9 about the youth uprising in France and the role being played by trade unions and the revolutionary left.

What were the immediate political results of the November 5 general strike called by French trade unions in response to cost-of-living pressures and public service cuts, which mobilised an estimated 1 million people or more?

Today [November 9], the prime minister [Sébastien Lecornu] met with union leaders for the first time in a while. This was a direct consequence of the mobilisation by high school students who strong-armed the unions to do anything. The prime minister said was willing to raise the minimum wage by 1.6 % (about €1502 a month), which is way below inflation.

There are eight national trade union confederations in France. Almost all local unions are affiliated to one of them. The politics of these eight confederations is shaped by history: for example, the CGT [Confédération Générale du Travail, General Confederation of Labour] used to be controlled by the Communist Party and was very strong in blue collar industries; the CFDT [Confédération française démocratique du travail, French Democratic Confederation of Labour] is more social democratic; the FSU [Fédération Syndicale Unitaire, United Trade Union Federation] almost exclusively covers teachers.

Some people divide them between “reformists” and “radicals”, but all defend the interests of their own bureaucracy rather than the interests of the movement. Some unions, such as the CFDT, say the wage hike is not high enough but believe the government is an honest partner and want to negotiate wages across different industries.

The CGT believes in negotiating but wants to convince the government that they cannot be ignored; that is why they have called a day of strikes and actions on November 17 to show off a bit of muscle. The CFDT has decided not to join the strike on November 17. The CGT called the November 5 strike just one month before, showing that they had no genuine desire to help the youth movement [which started in September], otherwise they would have called it sooner.

The spark for the general strike was the powerful movement of youth and students against the under-funding of the education system. Has it led to offers of further concessions from the French government, on top of previous offers given to youth and students? Is the government attempting to sideline the demands of organised workers and separate them from the students by appealing for “dialogue” with trade union leaders?

The prime minister invited youth organisations to discuss the future of education. Also present at the meeting was the far-right youth organisation UNI [Union Nationale Inter-universitaire, Inter-University Union] and several far-right MPs, so the left representatives walked out. We will not discuss anything in the presence of the far right.

There are several youth organisations and student unions, but participation in student elections is very low, generally only a few percent of students vote. They do not act as unions defending the immediate interests of students — though there are some exceptions at a very local level. Instead, they mainly act as political organisations defending a particular vision.

A few weeks ago, the education minister [Édouard Geffray] tried to calm the youth movement with scraps such as creating 15,000 additional higher education places. But youth organisations are asking for 260,000 new university spots.

The government is trying to divide workers and students, but many are not falling for it. Tomorrow [November 10] is a day of action and strike for both teachers and students.

How has the far-right Rassemblement national (National Rally, RN) reacted to the general strike and the movement overall?

This movement is polarising people. There are many instances of people reacting to police brutality against the youth. We have had almost as many police arrests of youth protesters in one month as we did in one year of Yellow Vest protests. But some workers are also saying the police should shoot the protesters.

Overall, it is a hard time for the far right because [President Emmanuel] Macron is kind of stealing their talking points: more police, more brutality, etc.

Can the movement effectively translate its anti-government activity against the Macron administration into anti-fascist action to confront the RN and far-right groups in the streets?

I feel we may not be there yet. In Montpellier, some fascists tried to organise their own “militia” to protect local stores against looting. They boasted that cops were working with them. The fascists have a lot of sympathisers in the police force, but the state is not really using them as its main tool at the moment.

But even without arming thugs to beat up workers, racism still kills: on October 23, a 26-year-old Black man was shot and killed by a far-right terrorist who wanted to target “Blacks and Arabs”. The far right clearly carries responsibility for this murder, and many others.

What is the role and status in these protests of the left-wing party La France Insoumise (France Unbowed, LFI), which is led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon? Does LFI tend to initiate protests and attempt to assert a leadership role in them, or do they simply seek to influence them?

LFI controls one student union, L'Union Étudiante [Student Union], and they are part of the movement, but it is an exaggeration to say that they or any other organisation controls it. The ruling class pushes this narrative to paint youth as incapable of leading their own struggle and claim someone must be “behind” all of this.

In reality, youth organisations in general are quite small. The leadership of the movement really belongs to the students themselves through their general assemblies and national coordinations. All the universities and high schools on strike send delegates to a national coordination, which sets the agenda and decides what to do to ensure that students control the movement, rather than any specific organisation.

[Abridged from LINKS — International Journal of Socialist Renewal.]

author: Tony Smith
title: AI breeds homogeneity — the antithesis of folk music
content:
For unique and indigenous cultural forms to survive and evolve, they need to withstand the homogenisation of cultures that is part of the process of global capitalism. For some cultures, geographical isolation, and the continuation of traditional farming practices allowed this.

Folklorists describe how communities living in isolated valleys or mountainous areas often have customs very distinct from those of their neighbours, due to differences in terrain and mode of production.

This phenomenon manifests in variations of songs, dance tunes and airs that are unique to specific groups and geographical locations.

But the growth of capitalism encroached upon indigenous and traditional ways of life, with industrialisation forcing rural populations onto the cities, and with mining and agribusiness destroying traditional modes of farming.

New forms of transport meant geographical distances could now be covered in shorter times. Mass communication facilitated the sharing and exchange of unique cultural practices, but at the same time introduced the cultural practices of ruling elites which often dominated local traditions.

Sometimes debates arise about ‘correct’ or ‘original’ versions of traditional folk tunes and songs. These arguments might not seem to have great importance — but folk musicians instinctively fear that their unique cultural practices and way of life is being threatened.

Folk musicians are concerned about the motives of outsiders who record or listen to their music. This distrust can inhibit the work of folklorists who are studying and preserving a song or tune in good faith.

The movie Songcatcher (2000) tells the story of a musicologist who finds versions of lost traditional English songs like Barbara Allen and Moonshiner preserved in the remote Appalachian mountains in the United States. These songs are then recorded and repatriated.

But problems arise when one particular version of a song or tune is recorded — either in audio or in musical notation — because it advantages one version over others.

For genuine folklorists, a tune or song is organic and mutable. It is the nature of folk songs to vary according to the occasion, the influence of singers’ moods, and whether a singer feels in good voice. There is no bland setting into stone and this is part of the excitement of folk music.

Folk song collectors with integrity acknowledge multiple versions. On the Mainly Norfolk site for example, most songs are presented with at least two interpretations.

Folk singer Shirley Collins warns that commercialisation brings compromise. In her memoir All on the Downs, Collins explains that commercialisation means songs and singers lose integrity, and a sense of the genuine and the vital connection between songs and places.

A feature of folk music is the direct, oral transmission of songs and tunes. Considering her role in the tradition, Collins reckoned that when she sang, she felt generations of folk singers standing behind her, and became a “conduit for their songs, a link in a mysterious chain ... responsible for maintaining their integrity”.

Shirley Collins’ experiences should be compulsory reading for anyone interested in the preservation of folk traditions. When we hear folk music we easily imagine a specific landscape, its flora and fauna and its people. This is something that cannot be bought or imposed from outside. It touches our inner beings.

Paradoxically, one of the ways traditional music survives is that folkies (folk musicians) write new material. This is not only permissible but it is important for maintaining traditions. When folkies write new songs and tunes, they respect traditions and work within its broad bound.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) does not respect traditions but exploits them, mimicking them for commercial reasons. Difference is everything in the folk tradition. AI, however, smooths out wrinkles and obliterates individuality.

Consider Mick’s Misfortunes, a series of AI generated folk-style songs on YouTube. Ironically, most of Mick’s difficulties relate to aspects of his life forced upon him by technological changes. In these songs, the lyrics are fine, but the production is so uniform that it reduces everything to a bland mass.

Feeling the essence, rather than merely observing as an outsider is important in folk music. There is no evidence that AI understands sentiment.

APRA AMCOS (Australian Performing Rights Association / Australian Mechanical Copyright Owners Society) published its AI and Music report in 2024, detailing what they described as the ‘devastating’ impact of AI on original work, predicting that close to a quarter of revenue is being lost by legitimate copyright holders.

The AI and Music report expressed opposition to AI’s mining of original material, and also included results of a survey of its members on the topic. Many APRA AMCOS members told the survey that their livelihood was under threat, and that governments were not doing enough to prevent exploitation and theft.

89% of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander members surveyed for the report said that “AI has the potential to cause cultural appropriation” and 67% agreed “that using AI in music creation makes it harder to protect their cultural rights".

APRA AMCOS, along with other music, media and creative industry organisations on November 18 launched the Not AI’s To Take campaign, which calls on the Australian Government to “keep existing copyright protections in place” and says Australian creative work should not be used without permission and agreed payment.

While folkies with original material might expect their copyright to be respected and even to get some credit from the performing rights association when people use their material, they can forget it in the case of theft by AI. Respected Australian folkies Penny Davies and Roger Ilott recently announced that they would no longer post lyrics on their website, fearing they would be mined by AI.

AI companies surely see folk music with its innate idiosyncrasies, as an area for polishing, with the aim to make profits. For folkies, this amounts to wilful destruction of a culture that AI does not understand. The process is reminiscent of the robber barons of nineteenth century imperialism –including their claims of moral superiority and their disdain for Indigenous peoples.

AI is built on inequality and arrogance, and, as Rezgar Akrawi argues in a recent Green Left article “on accumulated human knowledge and on the labour of millions”. It is difficult to see any good resulting except to a rich minority.

Like all cuckoos, AI will not be content to have their versions in the nest alongside the original works. Having taken up a position on the internet, the next logical step is for it to destroy its competitors.

The problem is that this is not just likely to affect material which is online. It will diminish the space available at festivals, clubs, dances and pubs. It will destroy the incentive for people to meet in garages and on verandahs. The future of living musicians and real music is threatened.

[Dr Tony Smith is a former academic who has devoted himself to folk music for two decades.]

author: Önder Algedik
title: COP31 collapsed in Türkiye. The hosts’ fossil ties did not
content:
The COP31 talks in Antalya ended on November 22 without a decision. It was the first such failure since Copenhagen in 2009. In Australia, the argument is about Chris Bowen.

Here is what the argument leaves out.

Saudi Arabia kept a fixed position through the second week: The text must not mention fossil fuels and should boost carbon capture, delegates told Reuters. NPR reports that Saudi Arabia and Russia blocked fossil fuels from the final agreement. The European Union (EU) also hardened its position, according to Reuters.

The rejection came from the other side.

The EU, several small island states and other vulnerable countries said they could not accept a text that failed to mention oil, gas and coal. Ireland’s climate minister, speaking for the EU, said the COP was “hijacked by some oil states”.

Vanuatu’s delegation called the silence on fossil fuels unacceptable. Least developed countries and the African Union also objected over finance, accusing the EU of failing to honour past commitments. The Marshall Islands delegation said the Pacific was “let down on all sides”.

The people who said no to a text without fossil fuels were the people most exposed to them. They are not the people who wrote it that way.

Saudi, Chinese and Russian officials frequently visited the presidency offices, as Saturday became Sunday, delegates told Reuters, while other groups struggled to secure meetings.

Negotiators from Europe, small island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa said Saudi Arabia had disproportionate access. The Turkish presidency said no group or country received preferential treatment!

I cannot prove a link between what Türkiye signs and who gets a meeting. The ties themselves are public. Türkiye and Saudi Arabia signed a renewable energy agreement worth about US$2 billion in February. It entered into force on October 21 and a further memorandum was signed in Antalya on November 10, witnessed by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.

On November 5, four days before COP31 opened, the Turkish parliament ratified the Mecca defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, by 279 votes to 119.

Then, the day after the COP31 talks collapsed, the Russian gas corporation Novatek’s chairperson said in China that it had signed an liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply contract with Türkiye. The counterparty, volume and term were not disclosed.

Türkiye presided over COP31, through Murat Kurum, its environment, urbanisation and climate change minister. Australia led the negotiations, through the Climate Change and Energy Minister Bowen, with “exclusive authority ” over them.

That matters more than the blame game in Canberra suggests.

Bowen’s 18-page draft of November 16 called for a phase-out of fossil fuels. By Thursday, it was nine pages without fossil fuels and the Pacific Resilience Facility Australia had championed.

Bowen presented the final text with Kurum. The ABC’s Laura Tingle reported that he conceded red lines on fossil fuels and finance had blocked a deal. She also noted that Türkiye effectively set the conditions while Australia carried the negotiating burden.

Coalition Opposition leader Angus Taylor, who wants Australia to scrap its already weak net zero targets, said Bowen should resign. Albanese answered by invoking the national interest. Nobody mentioned the coal and gas mine expansions.

Australia was named Fossil of the Day as the first draft came out, with the Climate Action Network counting 38 coal and gas approvals since 2022. On October 14, the federal government approved 30 million tonnes more coal at Boggabri, until 2040.

Most emissions from such projects occur overseas.

One host approves projects. The other signs contracts. The units differ; an approval is not a contract. The direction is the same.

By my count, Türkiye has signed 19 fossil fuel agreements since September 2025, plus six nuclear and mining deals, which I count separately. Novatek would be the 20th. In the venue, 103 fossil fuel and polluting organisations registered. Sixty were fossil fuel interests and 45 came as Türkiye’s guests.

For the Pacific and the vulnerable countries, the talks’ collapse is a loss they can name. For the fossil order it costs nothing. It can lose a text. It cannot afford to lose a mine, a pipeline or a contract that runs for decades and none of those were on the table in Antalya. A text decides what governments agree to say. Approvals and contracts decide what they do.

So the useful measure of COP31 is not whether a paragraph survived. It is what was approved or signed while it was being drafted. By that measure, the summit did not fail the fossil order. It worked.

Our demands are structural: No new coal, oil or gas projects, starting with the extensions in Australia’s approvals queue and the contracts on Türkiye’s desk; an end to fossil fuel subsidies; public ownership of energy; free public transport.

These are the demands of a climate revolution, not of a better summit.

Count the approvals. Count the contracts. Then write the text.

[Önder Algedik is a climate researcher and activist with 350Ankara. His new book, Ya Fosil Düzen Ya Devrim (Fossil Order or Revolution), is published by İletişim.]

author: Pip Hinman
title: Labor’s new ‘defence’ bill a threat to democracy
content:
The federal government's new “defence” bill shows the lengths to which Labor is prepared to serve its senior partners in AUKUS, particularly the United States.

The Defence Legislation Amendment (Accelerating Capability and Protecting Bases) Bill 2026, which passed the Senate on November 19 with support of the Coalition, One Nation, Jacqui Lambie and Ralph Babet, hands “extraordinary new powers” to the defence minister, foreign militaries and private companies, Amnesty International said.

David Pocock, Lidia Thorpe, Fatima Payman and the nine Greens Senators opposed the bill in the Senate, and every crossbench MP backed the call for a longer inquiry.

The bill expands the defence minister’s power to establish “security zones”, which restrict public access to places it has designated to be areas of national security. The minister can authorise a senior public servant to simply declare any sea, land or airspace a “defence security zone”.

It allows the minister to override state and territory laws.

It introduces draconian penalties — including up to 15 years’ imprisonment — for “a person who commits an offence”. Activists, journalists and anyone else who stumbles anywhere near these security zones can be criminalised.

Amnesty said people could be detained even though they may not know the exact boundaries of the declared security zones.

Defence minister Richard Marles is trying to downplay the bill’s reach and significance. But he admits the bill is aimed at squaring Australian laws with the government’s commitment to the US and British war pact, known as AUKUS Pillar I and II. As he put it: “Australia’s strategic circumstances demand urgency.”

Labor has avoided taking the unpopular AUKUS deal to an election. It has also restricted parliamentary scrutiny on this controversial bill to just a few days.

The Point has listed six alarming aspects of this bill. They include giving the minister and certain public servants the power to make “capability declarations” which override state, territory and federal laws. These declarations do not have to be made publicly available. They can facilitate weapons testing — including by foreign militaries.

A public servant could “switch off” state laws so that a foreign military could test their weapons here. The bill does not specify which laws can be overridden, but as The Point notes, it will be the “inconvenient” ones such as environment or heritage protections.

The penalties for those wishing to protest are steep: fines range from about $4000 to more than $150,000; 37 of the offences appear to carry prison sentences, ranging from 12 months to 15 years.

“Most of those offences include ‘strict liability’ or ‘absolute liability’ for some elements. This means that prosecutors only need to prove that you did something, not that you meant to do it. It also means that very few defences are available.”

You can be “reasonably suspected” of committing an offence in relation to a defence zone and be detained, including by a weapons’ contractor for the Department of Defence.

Lawyer Rita Jabri Markwell has also pointed out that the bill dovetails with Labor’s ambition for artificial intelligence data centres and AI’s role in the Five Eyes’ surveillance work. She said the new law will make it “harder to hold universities to account for their complicity in developing technology that enables companies and forces to commit war crimes”.

It will also make it harder for Traditional Owners to stop weapons testing on Country; to stop the contamination of their land and water and for any of their Country to be used to store radioactive waste. The First Nations fact sheet makes clear that the Woomera Prohibited Area remains a military zone, despite local First Nations opposition.
