author: Gwenael Velge
title: Behind the myth of the green data centre
content:
A recent Guardian article provides a glimpse into what good practice looks like when it comes to data centres: The EcoDataCenter’s 80 MW facility in Falun Swede is built from timber, runs on hydro and wind power and pipes its waste heat into the town’s district heating.

Yet, the article concludes with a hollow cliché — there are better and worse ways to do data centres. This really means that there are better and worse ways to do capitalism.

How many data centres the world needs is largely a question of demand, we are told. “How much more AI do we require, and how much do the benefits offset the harms?,” the Guardian asked.

Which community, river or forest “demands” hyperscale data centres?

What is posed as a neutral given — supply and demand — is really a political choice set by capital looking for returns. The cost, however, eventually falls on people and ecosystems at the local and planetary level.

For this exact reason, the Falun project deserves attention. The local council there started the project in 2010, years before the AI boom. Suppliers were local, the power is renewable and the waste heat warms homes.

Falun’s origin shows that when a community plans infrastructure around its needs and resources, it can do it well. It does not show that hyperscale data centres are either necessary or “sustainable”.

The article provides us with useful ratios for Falun: A power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.15 against a European Union average of 1.36; a carbon usage effectiveness (CUE) of 1.17 grams per kilowatt-hour against 414 in the United States.

These numbers speak of efficiency per unit. But we are never provided with a total and that is what we must consider if we are to tackle global warming.

The primary question should be how much heat and emissions can we afford; how efficient each unit is comes second.

Getting it the wrong way around leads to a paradox in which efficiency feeds growth.

In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons pointed out that more efficient steam engines did not reduce Britain’s coal use; they increased it, because cheaper power found more uses.

The same logic applies to computing. Political economist Grace Blakeley points out that Morgan Stanley’s forecasts of US data centre power demand already include Nvidia’s next generation of far more efficient chips and still projects a shortfall of 107 gigawatts (GW) — 18 New Yorks worth of electricity — by 2029.

Efficient computing is cheaper, which expands demand, which requires more power, which generates more waste — heat, emissions, tailings and pollution.

Aren’t these “sustainable data centres” powered by renewables though?

The historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz has shown that there has never been an energy transition; there has only ever been energy addition.

Coal did not replace wood: Britain used more timber to prop up its coal mines than its whole economy had burned as fuel a century earlier. Humanity burns more wood, coal, oil and gas today than at any point in history.

Under this historical-material lens, renewables are simply one more source of energy for accumulation, not a means towards energy transition.

In Thermal contradictions of electronic capital, Grégoire Chamayou traces a similar computing history. Each time chips hit a thermal wall, engineers find a fix: cooling fins, air conditioning, cooler chip designs and now immersion in liquid.

The engineering fix solves capital’s eternal problem — falling profitability — so that accumulation can resume and reach a higher peak. In effect, the engineering fix is to increase the speed at which the thermal cost can be externalised into the surrounding eco-social environment.

Data centres are a case in point; they are literally “hyperscaled heat machines”; all the energy that goes in comes out as heat.

In other words, accumulation is exponentially costly, it must find forever more efficient ways to externalise waste.

On a finite planet, this runaway waste accumulation eventually meets hard physical limits — planetary boundaries.

Under the accumulation paradigm “efficiency” and “sustainability” are themselves co-opted and become a means for further accumulation, whether materially via engineering fixes, or rhetorically as legitimating spin.

What the system refuses to acknowledge is the material absurdity of exponential growth.

The physicist Tom Murphy has calculated that even if we had a magic wand and solved carbon emissions today, yet kept growing at 2.3% a year, waste heat alone would bring the Earth’s surface to boiling point in about 400 years.

Exponential growth on a finite planet is simply not among the material possibilities, for anyone, whatever the technology.

Falun’s expansion is a case in point.

The sustainability officer reports that: “[O]ur core components into what we sell are land and power. It’s a very linear business in that way. It’s very hard to have exponential growth because we work with physical constraints.”

Yet EcoDataCenter’s next site, in Borlänge, is three times larger (240 MW).

Meta is building a 723 MW facility in Luleå, Sweden; Brookfield plans 750 MW in Strängnäs, Sweden, and Google has broken ground in Horndal, Sweden. All profess to follow the “Nordic model”.

EcoDataCenter’s sustainability chief says hyperscalers are “definitely needed in the ecosystem”. Why? We aren’t told.

As long as accumulation is the goal, a “sustainable hyperscale data centre” is little more than greenwashing. It is an example of profit without corresponding socio-physical costs.

A “sustainable data centre” is tantamount to “sustainable mining” or “sustainable capitalism”. It is a story we’d like to believe, but which has no historical precedent or material grounding.

Consequently, the burden of proof belongs with those promising green growth and “sustainable heat machines”. Why and how will this time be any different?

Meanwhile, the questions that actually matter are: What should we use our limited energy budget for and how should it be distributed?

The irony is that Falun’s virtues came from public planning, not from the market. A council designed it to serve a town; capital now holds it up as proof that profit-seeking hyperscale data centres can be green.

How much to build is a political question and it requires a political answer. There is no such thing as abstract “demand”; there is capital demanding growth while people and ecosystems demand a liveable planet.

[Gwenaël Velge is a research associate with the Mineral Policy Institute and School of Humanities and Social Sciences at Murdoch University. He is a member of Socialist Alliance.]

author: Binoy Kampark
title: Floods add to severe humanitarian crisis in Gaza
content:
Palestinians in the Gaza strip continue to live in precarious conditions, accommodated in makeshift, overcrowded shelters and tents brought about by a war waged with catastrophic consequences.

Israeli authorities are resisting efforts to improve living conditions in Gaza, even as they advance the demarcated Yellow Line that is shrinking the already diminished territory.

Heavy rainfall since November 6 has added to the misery for Gazans, 65% of whom live in tents or rudimentary shelters. Just under 1 million people live in areas prone to flooding, with 400,000 living in areas determined by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as “extremely high risk”.

Tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians have been flooded.

Instances of respiratory illnesses are on the rise. “The numbers already show the pressure,” Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said. “Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year.”

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the rains “damaged displacement sites, shelter and humanitarian facilities, and disrupted services across all five governorates”.

The damage caused within 24 hours was formidable, affecting 26,000 households. (That number has since risen to 46,000.) More than 6000 family shelters were destroyed in that time, with 17,400 damaged. Damaged buildings have collapsed, and the rains have added to existing structural and environmental risks.

Adding to this are the problems of exposed ordnance buried under the debris or shifted to other areas, endangering the lives of residents and humanitarian personnel.

The November 13 humanitarian situation report from OCHA is evenly grim. Between November 3–9, Israeli airstrikes, shooting and shelling continued, killing 22 Palestinians and injuring 90.

This brought the total number of reported deaths since the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement to 1613, with 5833 suffering injuries. The Ministry of Health in Gaza retroactively added 12 fatalities once their identification details were verified.

But there has not been a rise in humanitarian supplies to cope with the rain-borne crisis — rather the opposite. Between November 2–8, 228 of the 262 United Nations and partner trucks intended for entry into Gaza were offloaded on the Israeli side of Kerem Shalom; 128 from Ashdod, 25 from Egypt, 44 from Israel, 12 from the West Bank and 18 from Jordan.

The OCHA reported that the number of trucks offloaded constituted a fall of 42% from the previous week. Israel suspended the Egyptian corridor, citing concerns over smuggling. Between November 3–8, no trucks were offloaded.

The overall figures also fell due to, in the UN agency’s words, “reduced aid volumes available to partners amid funding constraints”.

The Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), responsible for coordinating aid, says otherwise. The crisis is being addressed; poor sanitary conditions were being improved prior to the rain, an effort coordinated with international bodies. More than 93,000 tents and over 8600 trucks holding tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the winterization plan was launched by the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs.

But the Haaretz newspaper obtained data which revealed a growing decline in food deliveries to Gaza, to add to severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair crippled infrastructure.

Under the ceasefire deal, Israel had pledged that it would permit 4200 vehicles carrying essential humanitarian aid and commercial items, including food, fuel, vital medical equipment and supplies, shelter materials and equipment for repairing essential infrastructure into Gaza each week.

COGAT’s own figures supplied to the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) show totals well short of the promised monthly rate of 18,200 vehicles allowed into the Strip: 4700 in March, 5300 in April and over 9600 in May.

In June, the number rose to 12,000, only to fall again to 10,000 for the months of July and August. September proved to be the high point with 13,000, while in October only 6500 vehicles were allowed in. (Seemingly caught out by this unusual affliction of verisimilitude, COGAT called its own figures “inaccurate”, saying that Israel had met and even exceeded its humanitarian commitments.)

COGAT’s mangled version of reality has not impressed some foreign ministries. In its November 14 statement, the Council of the European Union expressed concern that flooding and wintry conditions were “further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering”.

The Council also noted the lethal strike on Nasser Hospital by the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) that killed six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy.

Israel was urged “to allow immediate, unimpeded access and sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance and early recovery support at scale, and to reopen all Gaza border crossings”.

A few days later, a joint statement from the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom warned that “as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire”. It said 150,000 tents, along with other essential supplies were “being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza. The situation is entirely reversible – and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in.”

They called on Israel “to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza”. The crossings had to be opened, and tents permitted to enter. “Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late.”

Van De Weerdt said of the crisis that promises to deteriorate: “It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come.”

[Binoy Kampmark currently lectures at RMIT University.]

author: Brett Wilkins
title: Israel extends imprisonment of Gaza doctor Hussam Abu Safiya for 6 more months
content:
Israeli authorities on November 18 extended the detention without charge of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, the former director of northern Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, for another six months, prompting outrage from human rights defenders and renewed calls for the release of the pediatrician and scores of other imprisoned Palestinian medical professionals.

According to Abu Safiya’s lawyer, Nasser Odeh, an Israeli court in Beersheba extended the 53-year-old’s indefinite imprisonment through May 2027.

“Why must I spend another six months away from my family?” Dr Abu Safiya reportedly asked the court, claiming he is being punished for doing his job.

According to Al Jazeera, the court justified the continued detention by declaring that Abu Safiya “poses a threat to the state of Israel.”

Israel claims Abu Safiya is a colonel in Hamas’ Military Medical Services and has shown a photo of the doctor wearing a uniform that Al Jazeera said belongs to the Palestinian Directorate of General Military Medical Services, an organization providing healthcare to Gaza security personnel and civilians. The Qatar-based news network said that wearing the agency’s uniform does not establish Hamas membership.

There is also a dispute over the word “colonel”. Critics of Israel’s allegation say this is a professional or honorary designation within the medical services, not proof of a Hamas military command position, much like the United States surgeon-general is not an actual general.

The court’s decision came despite mounting international concern over Abu Safiya’s health and treatment in Israeli custody.

“The information that we are receiving about the health conditions of my father and how he’s being treated is very concerning,” Elias Abu Safiya, the imprisoned doctor’s son, told Al Jazeera on November 12. “My father weighs only 53 kilograms now, and he’s been suffering from very harsh conditions, three floors underground. He is in a solitary room, deprived of food, water, and medicine.”

Elias Abu Safiya continued: “We know he’s been subject to torture and bad treatment. My father still has some shrapnel stuck in his body, and he’s not seen a surgeon. This is inhumane, very harsh conditions that not even animals should be living in inside Israeli prisons. To add to this, he’s not been charged with anything. I don’t know why he’s being tortured this way. He’s a doctor, not a criminal or a murderer. He doesn’t deserve to be treated this way. The court denied the appeal to release him and 14 other doctors.”

Last week, Israel’s Supreme Court rejected a petition seeking the release of Abu Safiya and those 14 doctors, who are also imprisoned without charge or trial.

In July, the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights urged Israel to release the doctor immediately, or charge him and hold a fair trial. OHCHR said there were indications that Abu Safiya had been tortured and subjected to other abuse, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in serious injuries, and denial of medical care.

Abu Safiya’s 15-year-old son, Ibrahim Abu Safiya, was killed in an Israeli drone strike at the entrance to Kamal Adwan Hospital, where he was sheltering with his family, in October 2024. The following month, Abu Safiya suffered severe shrapnel wounds during yet another Israeli drone strike on the facility.

Israeli troops detained Abu Safiya on December 28, 2024 amid a prolonged siege and assault of the hospital after the director defied a forced displacement order and refused to evacuate the facility as long as patients were still being treated.

Former detainees released from Sde Teiman, the notorious torture prison in southern Israel, said they saw and met Abu Safiya there. According to testimonies collected by the Geneva-based Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, Abu Safiya was tortured prior to his arrival at Sde Teiman, and also while imprisoned there.

A United Nations commission concluded in 2024 that “Israel has perpetrated a concerted policy to destroy Gaza’s healthcare system as part of a broader assault on Gaza” that has left more than 250,000 Palestinians dead, maimed, or missing. The commission — which separately found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — further accused Israeli forces of “committing war crimes and the crime against humanity of extermination with relentless and deliberate attacks on medical personnel and facilities.”

Responding to the extension of Abu Safiya’s imprisonment, Amnesty International USA said on November 18 that the doctor “is being held without charge, separated from his family, his colleagues, and the children he lovingly treated.”

“Israeli authorities must immediately and unconditionally release Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya and all other arbitrarily detained Palestinians,” Amnesty added.

[Reprinted from Common Dreams.]

author: Chris Lang
title: The Antalya AI pledge: Voluntary commitments to greenwash a destructive industry
content:
The COP31 Presidency and the International Telecommunication Union, the United Nations agency for digital technologies launched the Antalya AI Pledge at COP31 in Türkiye, on November 16.

The Pledge is yet another voluntary pledge produced over more than three decades of COP meetings that will do less than nothing to address the climate crisis. Worse, the governments endorsing the Pledge are actively supporting a massively polluting industry that is accelerating the climate crisis.

The Antalya AI Pledge was launched at a “High-level Green Digital Action Roundtable on AI”. The Roundtable discussion is available here.

Tomas Lamanauskas, the deputy secretary-general of the International Telecommunication Union told the meeting that, “AI is really the technology that’s transforming our lives and mostly for good, I should say. From our daily ability to write speeches ... to much more high level aspects from medicine to agriculture, to education, as well as industries.”

Obviously, Lamanauskas didn’t give any concrete examples of any of this. Neither did he mention that the AI bubble is threatening another global financial crisis. Or that the main use of AI is to extract ever more fossil fuels. And he made no mention of the military AI industry.

“It has a really transformative potential to make everyone’s lives much better,” Lamanauskas said. Presumably Lamanauskas is oblivious to the recent United States elections in which voters made their feelings crystal clear about the data centres that have devastated so many communities.

Lamanauskas talked about AI’s energy use as a “challenge that we need to rein in if we want AI to sustainable power the world and to make sure that AI is a solution not the problem”.

Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, told the meeting that, “AI and other frontier technologies are a double edged sword. The task ahead is to blunt their dangerous edges, sharpen their catalytic ones, and put these technologies responsibly to work.”

Stiell noted that communities are “pushing back against data centres, concerned about their water, their energy bills, and their environment. So public support is already sinking deeper under water.”

Companies should, according to Stiell, “power data centres with renewable energy”.

But the Pledge makes no mention of fossil fuels. Instead it consists of vague statements about powering and building AI “sustainably”, managing AI “responsibly”, reporting the environmental impacts, and strengthening “financial support and technical infrastructure for AI for climate action”.

There is no mechanism to hold any of the companies or governments that sign the Pledge to account if they breach the terms of the Pledge.

The reality is that the Antalya AI Pledge is greenwashing a massively destructive, extractive, unethical, thieving industry. “AI companies’ license to operate is already on thin ice, right across political spectrums in many countries. And under that thin ice lie some potentially very deep regulatory waters, as political landscapes shift,” Stiell said in his speech at the launch.

“Very deep regulatory waters” is exactly what the world needs to prevent the damage that AI is already causing — damage that is accelerating every day.

“CEOs and boards need to step-up, and align business and investment plans with the world’s agreed climate goals,” Stiell said. The voluntary Antalya AI Pledge exists to allow the AI industry to continue its destructive business as usual.

Justine Calma, writing in The Verge, describes the Pledge as a “cruel joke”.

She points out that the Pledge even states that, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances”.

“In other words,” Calma writes, “these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims”.

On the same day as the launch of the Antalya AI Pledge, an assessment of the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres was published in Nature Sustainability. This is the first peer-reviewed estimate of the climate impact of data centres in the US.

The study estimates that hyperscale data centres in the US emitted between 21-31 million metric tonnes of CO₂ from May 2024 to April 2025 and used about 2% of US electricity. As Emily Atkin writes in Heated, these are big numbers, but “they’re also massive underestimations”.

Hundreds of hyperscale data centres were left out of the study because we simply do not know how many hyperscale data centres there are in the US

The electricity consumption isn’t the only problem with data centres. The equipment that keeps the servers in data centres from overheating leaks refrigerants that are potent greenhouse gases.

The researchers had to make assumptions about how the electricity powering the data centres was generated: gas, coal, renewables, etc. The researchers couldn’t tell how much electricity came from the grid and how much was generated from gas turbines built specifically to power the data centres.

And the study looked at data centres’ emissions in the 12 months up to April 2025. “The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025,” lead author Gianluca Guidi said in a press release. “New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

In August 2026, Business Insider and Insider Tech reported that there are 2228 new data centres currently planned or under construction across the US.

Atkin points out that she’s not criticising the study. “It’s clear the researchers did everything they could possibly do with the paltry information they had,” Atkin writes.

So far, only 10 governments have endorsed the Antalya AI Pledge: Andorra, Brazil, Colombia, Germany, Luxembourg, Republic of Korea, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Türkiye, and Uganda. Seven academic organisations have endorsed it, 21 civil society organisations, 47 companies, and seven other organisations.

The US, China, and the EU have not endorsed the Pledge. Neither have major AI companies such as Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, or Meta.

“The AI pledge risks giving Big Tech a green stamp without requiring it to address the real climate impacts of its infrastructure,” Jill McArdle, a campaigner with the Berlin-based organisation Beyond Fossil Fuels told Nature magazine.

Indigenous Climate Action, Mohawks United in Safety and Health, and Woven put out a response to the Antalya AI Pledge. They point out that, “Hyperscale data centers are actively threatening Indigenous communities such as Tonawanda and Akwesasne; hundreds of Filipino activists organizing against AI mega-center Pax Silica have been arrested in this past week alone; experimental AI surveillance is being weaponized against Palestinians; and rare earth mineral mining such as uranium in Dine Territory and lithium in Aranã Caboclo is proliferating- all to feed the AI machine.”

And they conclude that “Implementation of AI for climate change solutions without systemic change that prioritises Indigenous liberation and sovereignty, is a FALSE climate solution.”

author: Önder Algedik
title: COP31 week one: A summit without discussion of fossil fuels
content:
If you followed the first week of COP31 from Australia, you probably heard about the $32,000 coffee cart at the Australian pavilion and the hot mic that caught Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and energy minister Chris Bowen joking about where to keep their phones.

Much less was said about what happened in Türkiye on the opening day.

On November 9, while the summit opened with a lavish ceremony in Antalya, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan came out of a cabinet meeting in Ankara with good news: 135 million barrels of new oil potential had been found at Gabar, in Türkiye’s south-east.

The same day, at the HABAŞ steel plant in Aliağa, near İzmir, an overhead crane fell and ruptured a gas line. The explosion that followed killed 19 workers.

This workplace disaster did not make the agenda of the climate summit. HABAŞ runs its arc furnace on electricity from coal and gas, and supplies steel to the construction and car industries.

But COP31 does not talk about fossil fuels as a material order made of steel, cement and workers. It talks about an abstract “emission” to be managed from a distance. A worker killed in a fossil plant falls, by definition, is outside the frame.

Three days later, union confederations met inside the COP31 venue to discuss “just transition”. Nineteen workers were killed and Türkiye is speeding up its transition to fossil fuels but neither was on their agenda.

Türkiye, which holds the COP31 presidency, prepared well for a climate-changing summit. Since it was named host, it has signed 19 fossil fuel supply and exploration agreements, plus six nuclear and mining deals. It kept signing during the summit.

Australia, which presides over the negotiations, is no different. Labor had already approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects. Weeks before the summit it made it 38, clearing the Boggabri coal mine to dig another 30 million tonnes.

In Antalya, Albanese put the Pacific Island nations at the centre of his speech and then spent more time on home batteries than on coal and gas.

Bowen told the ABC that coal and gas exports have not damaged Australia's standing in the talks, and that his job is to land “the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow”.

Tuvalu’s Prime Minister Feleti Teo described new fossil fuel projects “a death sentence for us”.

The Pacific Resilience Facility, Australia’s showpiece, reached US$200 million in Antalya. By Albanese’s own account, 46% of the money, so far, has come from Pacific countries themselves.

Meanwhile, according to Climate Action Network, Australia has joined the European Union, Japan and Norway in opposing a commitment to triple adaptation finance, in the very text it is supposed to be steering.

This is what I call climate-changing policy. Once you know it, you can see the climate-changing summit behind the “climate summit” and the transition to fossil fuels behind the “just transition” slogan.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s environment minister, did not say the word “fossil” once in his opening speech. Bowen said it twice. At the leaders’ summit, Erdoğan and Albanese barely touched it.

In the first week, 56 negotiating documents were published; draft texts, informal notes, draft conclusions and decisions. They run to 268 pages. Coal and oil do not appear in them. “Fossil” turns up, at most, in a heading.

The only text that plainly mentions transitioning away from fossil fuels is a non-binding summary of views from the presidency. It repeats the 2023 Dubai sentence, limited to “energy systems”, so asphalt, cement and plastics are out from the start.

Brazil’s road map is voluntary. Even so, the Arab Group reportedly objected from day one to any reference to the road map in decision texts.

The words are missing because of how COP31 works. Decisions are taken by consensus, so a single bloc can strike it. The hosts are sitting on their own fossil expansion and have no wish to force it. The silence suits everyone.

Instead, Türkiye and Australia are selling another target: Lifting electricity’s share of final energy use to 35% by 2035. Whether that electricity comes from renewables or from fossil fuels is not the question. Bowen says tying it to renewables would be too hard for many countries.

Türkiye generates much of its own electricity by burning coal and gas, and Australia is among its top five coal suppliers.

The other big topic is finance: Extra money for climate projects, while the public keeps paying for the fossil order. Free public transport would cut urban fuel use sharply, and it is not on the table for discussion.

Next door, at the trade fair, you can buy green cement.

The hot topic among delegates for the first three days was traffic.

Antalya is the capital of Türkiye’s car republic: A city of 2.7 million with 366 municipal buses and three tram lines, carrying about 300,000 passengers a day. The summit registered 92,000 people. With one direction of the access road closed for official convoys, people spent three and a half hours covering 30 kilometres.

The fix? The governor sent schools online in seven districts for two days and put public servants on leave.

A city built for cars is a city that has guaranteed its fossil demand. Every jam is answered with more asphalt and more vehicles, and public transport is always postponed. The negotiating table works the same way and so do Australia’s car-built cities.

Kick Big Polluters Out counts 103 polluting companies and industry bodies with delegations at COP31. Sixty are from the fossil fuel sector. Forty-five came as guests of Türkiye.

The climate question is a coal, oil and gas question, and it is three wars at once.

There is a war over meaning, in which fossil fuels are renamed “electrification” and destruction “just transition”.

There is a war of capital over who sets the table.

And there is physical war: The attacks on Venezuela and Iran belong to the same fight over energy.

Australia and Türkiye fought on opposite sides in World War I. Today, they trade coal and gas, share a summit and wage war on the climate together.

If they will not talk about fossil fuels, we have to.

In Antalya, that means talking about free public transport and how we change the fossil order. In Australia, it means talking about 38 approvals and the coal ships, not the coffee cart.

Otherwise COP31 will be remembered as an exercise in populism and inaction.

[Önder Algedik is a climate researcher and activist with 350Ankara. His new book, Ya Fosil Düzen Ya Devrim (Fossil Order or Revolution), is published by İletişim.]

author: Maharnav Bhuyan
title: Labor and One Nation compete to arrest their way out of a mental health crisis
content:
Labor and One Nation agree on almost nothing, with the exception being on crime, where they read from the same script.

Premier Ben Carroll wants 1500 more police. One Nation wants more police, harsher treatment of repeat offenders and a 24/7 bail court. Its campaign launch promised to make Victoria the toughest state on crime. The Coalition has simply raised the bid to 3000. Labor's Attorney-General insists “tough bail is working”.

Victoria has run this experiment before. Labor funded 3135 more police between 2016 and 2021. Over 2024-25, the number of criminal incidents hit its highest level since records began.

Ask Victoria Police what drives crime and the answer reads like a social policy brief.

In June, it named the cost of living, recidivism, organised crime and drugs. In September, it listed organised crime, recidivism, mental health and illicit drugs.

Who ends up on the inside? In the latest national survey of people entering prison, from last year, 51% had been diagnosed with a mental health condition and 73% had used illicit drugs in the past year. In the month before prison, 43% were homeless and 46% were unemployed.

These statistics show that rather than being hardened criminals, prisoners are people who have been failed by a squeezed economy, a broken health system and by communities with nowhere to turn.

When people do reach out, the door is often shut.

About 4550 Victorians were waiting for drug and alcohol treatment on any given day last year. In June 2025, 14 men sat in custody waiting for a bed at Thomas Embling, the state’s secure psychiatric hospital. Victoria’s own royal commission found the mental health system had “catastrophically failed”.

On November 6, HungryPanda rider Feng Jianming was stabbed to death near the Queen Victoria Market. He was 47, a father of two, and had spent nine years working here to support his family. A second rider was seriously injured.

Roberto Urbano, 51, has been charged with the murder. He is presumed innocent, but the court has already seen something every politician promising more police should think about. Urbano’s lawyer told the court that he experiences schizophrenia.

Appearing by video link from a police cell, in front of a magistrate, Urbano stood on a stool and exposed himself to the courtroom. Police custody, a camera and a magistrate; there is no more heavily-policed place. If the law cannot reach a person in that state, another 1500 police officers on the street certainly will not.

People in a mental health crisis need care; they need treatment before things fall apart. Was Urbano seeing a doctor? Did he have somewhere safe to live? Those are the questions this case should prompt every party running in the election to answer.

None of this means people with mental illness are dangerous; they are several times more likely than others to be assaulted.

The lesson is simple: A society where vulnerable people can ask for help and get it is a safer society.

Instead, the money flows to prison cells. Since Labor’s “toughest bail laws in Australia” began in March last year, the prison population has grown by about 19%.

This year’s state budget found $229 million for new prison beds and $43 million for programs that keep people out of them.

Each prisoner costs the public purse almost $600 a day and more than a third of those released are back inside within two years.

One Nation’s other big idea — tougher sentences — is weaker still.

The Coalition offers more of the same. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson’s 3000 extra police would include recruits from Britain, Ireland and New Zealand.

The Coalition also promises a “one-strike” bail rule for serious offences and has promised to expand Adult Time for Violent Crime from eight offences to 20. Youth diversion gets a mention after the police, bail and sentencing pledges.

The Victorian Sentencing Advisory Council found that longer prison terms do not produce a matching increase in deterrence. A longer stretch inside does not treat what it was that put the person there.

You cannot handcuff the cost of living. You cannot arrest a mental illness.

This is not a call on parties to be “soft” on crime. It is about being more serious about crime prevention. That means funding mental health and drug treatment until the queues disappear. It means building the forensic beds, called for by the royal commission. People leaving prison need secure homes to go to. Nationally, a third expect to be homeless on release.

There needs to be investment in the struggling suburbs and towns, where disadvantage and prison admissions pile up.

Before buying another 1500 uniforms, find out why people end up in a cell.

Victoria should fund an independent, ongoing study that asks thousands of people in its prisons what went wrong in their lives, and tie prevention budgets to the answers.

Communities have shown another way. In Bourke, in north-west NSW, the Aboriginal-led Maranguka project, guided by the Bourke Tribal Council, has spent more than a decade shifting the focus from punishment to community-led solutions.

Labor and One Nation are selling the same police band-aid, but in different colours. Until we ask why are people ending up in a cell, the public will keep paying for more cells and more cops, and there will be more grieving families.

Before November 28, ask your candidates one question: What will you do before the crime, not after it?

author: Cas Smith
title: Hazelmere locals reject plans for mega AI data centre
content:
About 200 people rallied outside Midland Town Hall on November 11 to oppose plans for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data centre in Hazelmere, in Perth’s eastern suburbs.

Gwenaël (Gwen) Velge, a Research Associate at Murdoch University’s Mineral Policy Institute; Kate Herron from Trillion Trees; and former Labor MLA Matthew Hughes addressed the rally and highlighted the disruptive nature of CDC Data Centres’ planned project, which is expected to cause significant noise pollution and energy usage.

At a consultation meeting last month, a CDC technician said the data centre would have an energy allotment of 192 megawatts (MW) with 96 generators.

This would make it significantly larger than the 120 MW, 88 generator data centre previously proposed by Greensquare, which was rejected earlier this year by the City of Swan, following community backlash and concerns about noise pollution.

Velge noted the significance of this decision in the Mining Monitor on October 29. “Earlier this year, the City recommended refusing the GreenSquare proposal over the potential noise of its 88 generators.

“CDC proposes 96 generators, [which] come within 1dB (decibels) of the limit modelled at 75% load, and approach ‘the limits of compliance’; whereas Greensquare was asked to model at 100% load.”

He said the “sheer scale” of the energy demand of hyperscale data centres makes it harder to achieve a renewable energy transition.

“Renewable energy capacity meant to replace coal and gas is directly absorbed by this new demand. In the best-case scenario, this added demand slows down the transition, in the worst-case scenario the narrative and promises of ‘transition’ justifies and legitimates actual energy addition.

“Of course, some grid growth is to be expected as we electrify. But data centres are a clear case of addition: that demand did not exist before and it competes directly with the electrification part of the transition.”

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) expects consumption on the region’s electrical grid to increase by 57% in the next decade, from 20.4 to 32.1 terrawatt-hours (TWh).

However, this excludes the energy demands from data centre projects already in the pipeline, which are expected to be excessive, based on the ‘cooling’ requirement for servers.

Two planned projects in WA, the Hazelmere data centre and a project in Maddington — both proposed by CDC — are expected to consume 4.3TWh a year in total (or on a single hot day, up to 550–590MW).

Velge said this would be “more than five times AEMO’s forecast for the entire sector, and nearly 40% of the total projected growth for the next decade”.

“With huge amounts of heat comes huge amounts of emissions, and heat which must be displaced with either water or with fans.

“So, the choice is between huge water usage or noise. Adding this much extra demand on the grid is bound to push the price of electricity much higher than it already is.”

Another concern is the lack of transparency around the Hazelmere project, with many questions remaining about how it might develop. CDC’s application, for example, refers to the planned building as “HA1”, which raises the question: should people be expecting a HA2?

Local residents have discovered that CDC has acquired the adjoining lots at 170 Bushmead Road and 40 and 50 Hazelmere Crescent, making a larger project down the track a real possibility, even if the acquisitions had not been included in the current application.

This meant that CDC could be using a “salami-slicing” approach, splitting the project into smaller units, so that its cumulative impacts can’t be assessed as a whole.

In any case, Gwen argued that data centre projects should be approached like mining ones.

“Treating data centres like mining projects means applying our Mining Policy Principles: the right of affected communities to veto, assessment of cumulative impacts not just project by project assessments and a meaningful test of whether the project serves communities and the transition or if it serves private profits....

“We shouldn’t let ourselves be priced out of our own public utilities to release more carbon emissions and more heat into our globally warming atmosphere.

“As we know from the US, data centres are also an opportunity to rally people from all walks of life and all political stripes around something everyone opposes — a genuinely positive sight in the polarising times we live in.

“The numbers don’t add up. People and ecosystems will be left paying the price. We can still say no.”

author: Pip Hinman
title: NSW Labor goes full tilt to support coal
content:
As Yasmin Catley, police minister and NSW Labor MP for Swansea, in the Hunter, continues to rail about a climate protest she had wanted to ban, NSW Labor is rushing through a pro-coal bill which critics say undermines a recent federal High Court ruling.

The Paddle for the Planet, organised by Rising Tide, drew around 1000 people to Horseshoe Beach in Muloobinba/Newcastle on November 14. The protest was designed to highlight Australia’s lack of leadership at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye.

Its attendance was boosted by NSW Labor’s last-ditch undemocratic attempts to prevent it from going ahead. This included Premier Chris Minns’ direct intervention into Newcastle City Council, demanding it ban Rising Tide and, shockingly, “associates, subsidiaries, other groups and individuals” from holding events or protests on council land.

The motion only passed with the casting vote of independent Mayor Gavin Morris, after Labor councillor Declan Clausen crossed the floor to support the ban.

But the NSW Supreme Court’s decision to favour individuals’ right to peacefully express themselves knocked NSW Police’s efforts to ban the protest on its head.

At least 800 people took to the water in canoes and kayaks on a calm and sunny day. There was not one NSW Police officer in sight — nor any coal ships.

Climate activists occupied the channel for an hour to make their views known about Labor’s pretense over its commitment to the climate while approving new coal and gas projects.

Even after the peaceful event, Catley continued to rail against the climate activists for being “reckless” and “dangerous for everybody”.

Meanwhile, Cately and Minns are pushing a new pro-coal bill, favouring MACH Energy, which aims to circumvent a High Court decision on that company’s mine in the Hunter Valley.

The Environmental Defenders’ Office (EDO) described the Mount Pleasant Mine Bill 2026 bill, which went to parliament on November 10, as “eroding the rule of law, the separation of powers and public trust in independent decision-making”.

The bill, which Labor wants to push through this week, authorises MACH Energy to continue mining thermal coal at Mount Pleasant until 2032 (up to 16.5 million tonnes).

The EDO said not only does it override the pending process and decision of the Land and Environment Court of NSW, following the High Court decision, it contains a dangerously broad clause which allows the Planning Minister to be the consent authority for the approval, not the Independent Planning Commission. It would circumvent parliamentary scrutiny.

Jacqui Mumford, Nature Conservation Council NSW (NCC) CEO, said this “would give the Resources Minister unfettered power to override all other laws in relation to the Mount Pleasant coal mine” adding, “this kind of power is a major corruption risk”. She said such a law “would take NSW back to the days of [disgraced Labor MP] Eddie Obeid by bypassing independent assessments and public consultation”.

Labor’s talking points about “protecting jobs” at the Mount Pleasant mine are also being challenged.

While the bill contains a “jobs guarantee”, to which mining corporations must agree, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) pointed out that Labor has not shown a commitment to coal workers at Mount Pleasant, as most are on insecure labour hire contracts.

Labor signed off on a transition authority and investment fund which are supposed to support workers wanting to leave the fossil fuel industry. But with no dedicated funding figure in the Future Jobs and Investment Fund, it remains abstract.

Retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy and barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson have publicly criticised NSW Labor over its new coal bill. “I think it’s disgraceful,” Watson, a director at the Centre for Public Integrity and former senior counsel assisting the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, told The Guardian on October 21.

“This is, in effect, to overturn a decision of the high court of Australia after a fair hearing. In my book it’s contrary to the separation of powers which acknowledges that each branch of government has its own area or domain.”

Whealy told the ABC on October 20 that the government’s bill is “reprehensible” because it “obliterates” the legal process.

“With an election early in 2027, such matters do not seem to phase NSW Labor, which seems more singularly concerned about winning votes back from One Nation in coal mining regions,” Steve O’Brien, the Socialist Alliance candidate for Newcastle, told Green Left. “Of course, that could also be done by accelerating a just transition for fossil fuel workers to sustainable industries, plans for which have already been made over several decades.”

author: Wendy Bacon, Cathy Peters
title: Time to reassess the antisemitism envoy’s role
content:
Civil liberties and Palestinian supporters are calling for the Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, Jillian Segal, to be sacked after her latest report accused them of using “human rights” to hide their antisemitism.

Segal’s Plan to Combat Antisemitism appears designed to raise the pressure on all levels of government as well as the forthcoming final report of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion in December.

Segal is an active player in an international network, coordinated by key pro-Israel Jewish bodies as well as the United States State Department. Indeed, if it had not been for pressure from the US government, Segal might not have the job at all.

Segal is one of 32 Special Envoys in North America, Europe, South America, Israel and Australia.

The position of the US Special Envoy to Combat and Monitor Antisemitism was established in 2004, when New Jersey Republican congressman Chris Smith, who has a history of advocating for Israel and a record of accusing organisations including UN bodies of rampant antisemitism, successfully pushed to pass legislation creating the position.

Following the US lead, the European Union appointed an Envoy in 2015, followed by Canada, Greece, the Organization of American States and Britain. Israel’s envoy is part of its Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

In 2021, Smith, by then a strong supporter of Donald Trump, successfully pushed for an amendment which strengthened the position of US Special Envoy to the level of ambassador. They report directly to the Secretary of State, are appointed by the President and, crucially, can access foreign governments.

The ambassador’s mission is to promote US foreign policy by developing and implementing policies and projects to support action against antisemitism.

The office uses the controversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition, which directly links Jewish people with Zionism and the State of Israel, and conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism.

The current US Antisemitism Ambassador is far right winger Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun. He has boasted about influencing governments and recently described his office as supporting Trump’s policies by having 250,000 visas cancelled to keep campuses “‘safe”, interfering in foreign educational curricula and initiating prosecutions of what he describes as “hate crimes”.

This is echoed in Segal’s plan, which include compulsory training for Home Affairs staff responsible for certain visa applications and a new task force to review existing visas.

While it was initially reluctant, the Anthony Albanese Labor government appointed Segal in July 2024, after intense lobbying from the US State Department, which the Australian media did not cover.

FOI releases show that in May 2024, Aaron Keyek, the then US deputy antisemitism envoy, met with Australian officials in Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Attorney General’s Department to pressure the Albanese government to appoint an envoy.

Keyek also met with Deborah O’Neill, the Co-Chair of Labor Friends of Israel.

The crunch came with an ultimatum regarding a meeting of special envoys in Argentina, in July 2024, to sign US-drafted global guidelines to counter antisemitism.

A former senior US official told Jerusalem News Syndicate: “We were all diplomatic about it, but we told Australia, essentially, ‘It’s going to be glaring’. We didn’t want to repeat the situation, where one of our closest allies didn’t stand up to one of the top foreign-policy priorities when it comes to human rights that the United States is pushing internationally… So we told them that they could only attend if the delegation was led by a special envoy.”

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade sent a cable to the US State Department on July 4 advising of the imminent appointment of an envoy who would report directly to the Prime Minister.

Segal was appointed on July 9, just 10 days before the meeting in Buenos Aires, which she attended. According to that cable, she had already approved the guidelines and her tickets had been booked before she was appointed.

Australia’s Ambassador to Argentina was permitted to sign off on the guidelines which refer to the IHRA definition as a key tool for fighting antisemitism, as a result of Segal’s hasty appointment.

In 2019 the New York based World Jewish Congress (WJC), the central governing organisation of Jewish organisations, which “defends the Jewish state of Israel”, established the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Network to coordinate “responses to antisemitism”.

Segal’s work is partially dictated by this body. Since her appointment, Segal has worked closely with SECCA. In July last year, Rabbi Yehuda, the US Special Envoy in the State Department Ambassador thanked her for hosting an online forum.

In her first 15 months, Segal took five overseas trips, costing $85,000, and in May she travelled to Geneva to sign another SECCA joint declaration.

The 15th meeting of SECCA was held last month in Dublin, organised by the WJC in partnership with the European Commission. The conference aimed to look at ways to implement strong measures to “confront online hatred and turn government promises into concrete action”.

It heard reports from delegates from 28 countries, including Australia, and included visits to the European headquarters of TikTok and Meta. It included representatives from the WJC’s Technology and Human Rights institute, which focuses solely on lobbying governments, international bodies, and tech companies on policy, monitoring and control within the digital realm.

Maram Stern, WJC Executive Vice President and SECCA Co-Chair spoke at the forum emphasising the need to urgently enforce “practical solutions” to antisemitism.

Stern linked the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack to a worldwide surge in antisemitism, rather than to the worldwide revulsion with Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Segal. who spoke via video to the Dublin conference, urged stronger institutional accountability, education and enforcement against antisemitism.

Referring to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion (which heard many unchallenged allegations of antisemitism), Segal noted that its proceedings had brought into focus “concerns about antisemitism in universities, cultural institutions, and healthcare”.

These are key areas where we have seen false claims of antisemitism and lawfare used against academics, artists and healthcare workers.

Segal was not the only Australian who spoke. Her close partners from the Executive Council of Australian Jewry (EJAC), Peter Wertheim, EJAC co-CEO, called for “more proactive regulation of technology companies and effective legal avenues for people harmed by online content”.

Daniel Aghion, ECAJ president and WJC vice president, emphasised the importance of active special envoys, sustained government engagement and coordination between Jewish organisations.

Before the conference had started, it emerged that one of Dublin’s prestigious hotels had refused to accommodate the SECCA delegates and alternative accommodation and a conference venue had to be found.

This went unreported until Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, told a pre-conference event that the 4-star Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin, which had taken the SECCA booking for 70 rooms in April, had abruptly cancelled this booking after a meeting with the conference organisers and the hotel’s general manager.

Cohen was asked by the hotel manager whether the event had any ties to the Israeli Defence Force (IDF). He told Fox News Digital, “I was completely taken aback by that question. I said, ‘What would the IDF have to do with a conference on antisemitism?’.”

It was revealed that the hotel’s general manager subsequently consulted the hotel owners before the cancellation was made.

This was immediately characterised by the organisers as a major antisemitic event.

The World Jewish Congress published an opinion piece by Maurice Cohen on October 14 titled: “Ironically, an antisemitism conference falls victim to Jew-hatred”.

Although the Herbert Park Hotel refused to make public comment, it is clear it chose not to be associated with an event that had ties to the IDF.

The links between SECCA and support of Israel and members of the IDF are strong. SECCA representatives work with pro-Israel organisations, that have key personnel directly connected with the Israeli state, and past and present members of the IDF.

Conflating this refusal with antisemitism is yet another example of how peak pro-Israel Jewish organisations continue to wrongly link antisemitism to protest actions such as the Herbert Park Hotel boycott.

One of the major organisations participating in the SECCA conference in Dublin was the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM), which is based in the US and has spread internationally. Its advisory board members and its CEO are directly linked to Israel.

CAM works globally to pressure governments to not only endorse the IHRA definition of antisemitism but to enforce it. It reported that it was recognised as a “trusted US State Department partner” at the SECCA conference, where it reiterated the coordinated push to get governments to enforce the IHRA antisemitism definition — a point which was emphasised by US Special Envoy Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun.

CAM also has strong links with the IDF.

The J50 forum, founded by Israel’s foreign ministry, includes 50 Jewish organisations internationally. Its third meeting in Jerusalem last September issued its hard line and contentious Declaration on Zionism and Antisemitism, which stated unequivocally that “Zionism is part of Jewish identity”.

It defined anti-Zionism as a form of antisemitism when used to “marginalize or deny Jewish self-determination”.

Daniel Aghion’s presentation summarised ECAJ’s work since the Bondi terrorist attack. He offered some unguarded insights into how this organisation mobilised around the royal commission: “It has been a massive exercise over the last year. The Jewish community has spent millions of dollars, and many millions more in pro bono legal and non-legal work. This was to make sure that our voice is heard properly, both inside and outside the Commission, and to ensure that the Commission has run as well as it can.”

MWM asked ECAJ about whether any of ECAJ’s large government grants had been used on the royal commission work but not not receive a response.

On November 19, the Israel-based Jerusalem Post Group’s first Asia-Pacific Summit will be held in Sydney. It will feature many Israeli speakers, including Israel’s president Isaac Herzog’s wife Michel Herzog, who will speak online, the Israeli ambassador to Australia, former senior IDF members, as well as President of Zionist Federation of Australia, Jeremy Liebler.

The focus is on “countering hostility” to Israel and building business links, something which many anti-genocide Australians do not support.

Ten days later the 2026 CAM conference for mayors and councillors will be held in Sydney. These events reinforce the global messaging of SECCA, WJC and J50. They are designed to add impetus Segal’s agenda leading up to the first anniversary of the Bondi massacre, and prior to the release of the royal commission report in December.

Segal’s overreach into all aspects of our civil life is not just angering human rights activists, and those who are unfairly being labelled as antisemitic, but large sections of Australian society who do not support Israel and do not want to be policed at the service of this rogue state.

Albanese buckled to pressure in creating the position of antisemitism envoy and made a striking error in appointing the Israel lobby’s choice to that position.

As anger grows about Segal’s appointment, it is time to reassess the legitimacy of the position itself in light of the facts surrounding its creation.

We have existing anti-discrimination legislation and strong National Anti-Racism Framework guidelines that are yet to be implemented.

Bending to US, Israel and the local Israel lobby’s demands will only intensify public anger.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Protesters condemn state government attacks on Palestine solidarity, free speech
content:
Rallies were held across the country on November 15 to express solidarity with the people of Palestine and oppose repression of speech and protest by all levels of government.

The national day of action against repressive laws was called by Justice for Palestine Magan-djin (JFP) as part of its campaign to repeal the Queensland Liberal National Party government’s laws which criminalise Palestine solidarity slogans including “From the river to the sea” and “Globalise the intifada [uprising]”.

Chris Minns’ NSW Labor government is supporting the Queensland LNP government in the High Court challenge brought by JFP to overturn the laws. Victorian Liberals leader Jess Wilson has vowed to ban the phrase “Globalise the intifada” if elected on November 28.

JFP spokesperson Remah Naji said repression is “uniting our political class” and “thousands of us are united in defending our right to protest genocide”.

“The crimes remain the crime of genocide, the crime of occupation and the crime of apartheid. There is no amount of repression that will distract us from Israel’s crimes or absolve our government from its complicity in them.”

Michael Bradley, from MARQUE Lawyers, which is representing JFP in the High Court Case, said: “Queensland is currently leading the way with its ridiculous law that criminalises mere words, but other states are watching and keen to follow suit.

“It is more critical than ever that a stand is taken — in the courts and on the street — to demand our basic rights: to assemble, to protest and to speak.”

The crack down comes as Israel continues to kill Palestinians in Gaza and the Occupied West Bank, despite the so-called ceasefire. Its strike on the Nasser Hospital on November 12 — the only functioning hospital in Gaza — which killed six people, including surgeon Dr Rizq Shaira and a teenage patient, was condemned by 18 countries for violating international law.

As winter floods, storms and cold descend, many are still left sheltering in tents because of Israel’s restriction of supplies into Gaza. A nine-month-old baby died from hypothermia in Khan Younis in Southern Gaza on November 12 due to exposure to extreme cold.

Israel has killed at least 1610 Palestinians since the so-called ceasefire took effect.

Jonathan Strauss reports that 500 people marched in Magan-djin/Brisbane behind a large banner featuring the banned slogan “From the river to the sea”, a frequent chant of the Palestine solidarity movement.

The other banned slogan, “Globalise the intifada”, was not commonly used at Palestine rallies in Magan-djin, but expresses a desire for international support for the Palestinian people.

Anti-Zionist Jewish activist Stephen Heydt told the crowd that “kifah” means “fight” in Arabic. At the end of his speech he and others revealed t-shirts with the “globalise” slogan.

Police soon forcefully intervened, arresting seven people throughout the rally, including Heydt and two women who had carried the lead banner.

Naji said genocide was the real crime, not protesting the complicty of the Queensland and federal government.

The seven arrests add to the 31 previously made under the anti-free speech laws. Some, like Heydt, have now been arrested twice.

JFP is pursuing a High Court challenge to strike down the anti-free speech laws. It is asking for financial support for this and is organising a fundraising event on December 11.

The rally also featured music from a local punk band and a Riff Raff brass contingent.

Pip Hinman reports from Gadigal Country/Sydney that hundreds took to the streets again for Gaza on November 15. They demanded that NSW and federal Labor take action for Palestine, and stop trying to suppress free speech — particularly those speaking up against genocide.

The protest was called to show solidarity with pro-Palestine supporters in Queensland, who are being criminalised for standing up against genocide, and called for the scrapping of bans on phrases which call for rights, dignity, peace and justice for those living between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.

Minns wants to bring in similar laws, but is waiting on the outcome of the High Court challenge.

Speakers at the protest included Dr Shamikh Badra, who is from Gaza. He called on the federal government to act for Palestine, and not allow the weapons trade to continue.

Badra condemned the strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza. He said people were still being denied food, medical assistance and other aid, and recent floods had made their lives even more unbearable.

Sue Higginson, NSW Greens MLC, called on Labor to help. “The genocidal state of Israel will not let in the support. There are people [who have been] flooded, People have lost the only shelter they had — which was a flipping tent for goodness sake. And they can’t replace it.” She said Australia needs to impose a boycott, sanctions and divestment regime on Israel.

Meanwhile, foreign minister Penny Wong announced on November 16, that Australia had signed a joint statement with Canada, Italy and Britain urging Israel to allow “immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza ... before it is too late.”

Brian Mahony reports that protesters gathered in Gumbaynggirr Country/Coffs Harbour to join the November 15 national day of action to defend free speech and the right to protest.

Protesters also called for an end to Australia’s ongoing arms trade with Israel.

Cas Smith reports that about 300 people gathered at Russell Square in Boorloo/Perth on November 15 to call for an end to Israel's genocide in Gaza.

Speakers included Sarah Pickles from Right to Protest WA, primary school student Sakeenah Azizi, Palestinian-Australian Dareen Allagta, Sam Wainwright from the WA Anti-War Collective and Neda Blackwood from Teachers for Palestine WA.

The crowd were moved to tears by a performance from musical duo the Paddystinians — Johny Bravo and Ozzie Hishmeh.

A Paddle out for Palestine was held in Muloobinba/Newcastle on November 14, as part of Rising Tide’s Paddle for the Planet at Horseshoe Beach. Rachel Evans from City of Sydney for Palestine reminded the crowd that war and occupation is a climate issue.

NSW Greens MLC Sue Higginson said climate and Palestine protests are both being targeted by the Minns government’s undemocratic anti-protest laws. She said Newcastle City Council’s ban on Rising Tide events on council land would also apply to Palestine solidarity rallies.

title: Calvary takeover raises questions over hospital licences and access to VAD
content:
The proposed takeover of 14 former Healthscope hospitals by Catholic healthcare provider Calvary Health Care is facing scrutiny over competition, corporate accountability and the future availability of lawful healthcare services, including voluntary assisted dying (VAD).

Calvary’s proposed acquisition includes six NSW hospitals: Newcastle Private, Hunter Valley Private, Norwest, Lady Davidson, The Hills Private and The Sydney Clinic.

Calvary has confirmed it will not offer or facilitate VAD in any acquired hospital. Other excluded services under its Catholic healthcare guidelines include in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and assisted reproductive technologies, elective terminations, vasectomies, tubal ligation and gender care procedures.

The implications are particularly significant in the Hunter. Newcastle Private has an established role in providing VAD services. Go Gentle Australia reports that the hospital is understood to receive approximately one or two VAD requests each week.

Calvary says patients requesting VAD will continue to receive compassionate care and that appropriate pathways will be explored. However, transferring seriously ill patients elsewhere can create considerable practical, clinical and personal difficulties, particularly near the end of life.

title: Union slams Qantas’ plan to outsource 850 jobs
content:

title: Hundreds rally for AI data centre moratorium in Victoria
content:

author: Paul Gregoire
title: Karina Lester: ‘AUKUS is a radioactive waste nightmare’
content:
The AUKUS public inquiry released its final report on November 4. The five commissioners presented some stark realities about the “defence” pact between Australia, Britain and the United States, which is supposed to deliver eight Australian-owned nuclear-powered submarines (SSN).

A key issue the inquiry has brought to the fore is radioactive waste storage.

The AUKUS commissioners identified a massive cost — an estimated $180 billion — that taxpayers will have to foot, to store the radioactive waste.

This is on top of the $368 billion for the eight SSNs, which the inquiry said are not guaranteed to ever turn up.

The AUKUS report said that this additional, and never referred to, $180 billion outlay brings the total cost of AUKUS to around half a trillion dollars. It also advised that Australia has already gifted $3 billion to US and British submarine shipbuilding yards, with no guarantee of a refund if the deal collapses.

AUKUS Public Inquiry commissioner Karina Lester said that First Nations communities are concerned about the radioactive waste management plan, as there is no indication of where the waste site for highly-enriched uranium will be. It also remains highly volatile for hundreds of thousands of years.

Pillar I of AUKUS also establishes the Submarine Rotational Force – West, which involves US and British SSNs rotating out of HMAS Stirling, off the coast of Perth from 2027.

Even if the Australian-owned SSNs do not materialise, the Americans will have their own here at the ready.

The AUKUS commissioners recommended scrapping the AUKUS submarine deal entirely.

While Australia is expected to store its own waste, it turns out that the US and Britain have a decades-long issue of not being able to store their own waste.

Sydney Criminal Lawyers spoke to Karina Lester, one of the AUKUS Commissioners, who is a second-generation survivor of the British nuclear testing at Emu Field in South Australia.

The Yankunytjatjara Anangu woman said many First Nations communities are concerned about how and where the radioactive waste is going to be buried on Country, along with the fears over a base in Port Kembla.

The Surrendering Australia: The AUKUS Deception report clarifies many of the concerns about AUKUS. Fellow commissioner Peter Garrett told the National Press Club that the $368 billion works out to be $33 million a day for the next 30 years. He noted an additional estimated $180 billion will go towards managing radioactive waste disposal — a largely unaddressed aspect of the AUKUS deal. This is of particular significance to First Nations peoples.

What did the inquiry uncover regarding the storage of radioactive waste?

The AUKUS Public Inquiry found that it will be Australia’s responsibility to store the nuclear waste produced by these nuclear-powered submarines. The detail is yet to be defined or worked through.

Currently, Australia is going through a consultation process run by the Australian Radioactive Waste Management Framework. Last week, it was having consultations, which will provide feedback and clarity around waste management. But this was not about site selection.

From a First Nations perspective, if the AUKUS agreement says it is Australia’s responsibility to store this nuclear waste, we are concerned it will be stored somewhere in the outback, as we heard from former minister Kim Beazley. This, of course, will be First Nations traditional lands. So we are concerned about this.

At this stage, there is no site for the waste. But we’ve heard from defence minister Richard Marles that it will be somewhere on defence land, or future defence land. But there are no guidelines around where that future defence land will be.

At this stage, we know that we are responsible for the nuclear waste. This will be weapons’ grade nuclear waste, which will be concerning, as the waste will be high level and out on First Nations traditional lands.

So, there are unknowns coming out of the public inquiry and one of those is the site for nuclear waste.

When Marles refers to “future defence land”, does this mean that they could choose anywhere that is not currently defence land?

Yes. And there are no guidelines or criteria around how that selection process is going to be done, or where the future Defence land could be.

As Traditional Owners in South Australia, we have what is known as the Woomera Prohibited Area. That area is south of where my traditional lands are.

I’m up on the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara lands. The bottom end of those lands touch into the Woomera Prohibited Area. This is a fairly large area that is used for rocket launching. It is from the mid-north of the South Australian state, around Pimba and Woomera. It goes off into a north-westerly direction, which is currently defence land.

The site could also be on future defence land. So, there are some unknowns around this. This includes site location, number of sites and whether it is low- or high-level nuclear waste.

The public inquiry was unable to find out the answers to these questions.

The US and Britain have had these types of nuclear-powered submarines for decades but have not developed permanent sites for their waste disposal. What will it mean for Traditional Custodians to have such matter buried on Country?

The United Kingdom hasn’t dealt with its waste. We know there are nuclear-powered submarines docked in their shipping yards containing this waste that have been sitting there for quite some time.

We know that the US has also struggled with issues around safety and management of its nuclear waste.

So, this raises concerns from a First Nations perspective. No location has been identified, we don’t know where the waste is going to go and we also don’t know whose waste it is going to be.

The AUKUS agreement says it will be Australia’s nuclear waste. But there is a real fear from mob in South Australia, that it will be opened up to bringing in UK and US nuclear waste.

These are the fears and concerns we have. Again, it would be highly enriched uranium, the weapons grade uranium, which is of real concern.

When you do have highly enriched uranium, it does add a complex layer around keeping the waste secure and managing the facility. As Peter Garrett, our lead commissioner pointed out, there is an additional question around who is going to pay for managing this waste facility.

This is in addition to the $368 billion for the submarines. The cost of waste will be around $180 billion. That estimate involves identifying a location, building the facility, additional infrastructure and, potentially, having security there as well.

The AUKUS deal involves establishing the Submarine Rotational Force – West at HMAS Stirling, on Noongar land, off the coast of Perth in Western Australia. It appears to be shaping up to be a US submarine base, involving vessels that may be carrying nuclear warheads.

Despite SRF-West being slated to start next year, USS Colorado, the US submarine, is parked there now. How do you see HMAS Stirling?

When you know that a US submarine is currently docked there, it certainly looks like it is [a US base]. There is a real concern, which was echoed by many throughout the public inquiry, that Australia itself, as a nation, will potentially be a US base.

We know there are already US operations here, such as Pine Gap [in the Northern Territory], Tindall, also in the north of the NT and there is a potential eastern base, possibly located at Port Kembla, as well as HMAS Stirling off the west coast.

There is real fear that Australia is turning into a US base. That was made loud and clear from locals in WA, the NT and also, from the east coast in Port Kembla.

The inquiry heard from people living on Dharawal land in the NSW town of Port Kembla. There are fears that another US base might be established there.

How are the locals in Port Kembla preparing?

The Port Kembla community is very concerned about becoming a US base. This was a strong message. Many women were concerned about their safety and that of the children. So, there is an uneasy feeling because no decision has yet been made around whether Port Kembla will become a US nuclear base.

People have been talking about identifying a location on the east coast, where submarines could rotate. Port Kembla is a busy port currently. The commissioners considered how busy the port is to get an idea of how a US base with nuclear-powered submarines could be located there.

This is going to be an ongoing conversation.

After hearing more than 150 testimonies, what do you think the AUKUS deal is all about?

One of the strong messages coming from the inquiry is that the AUKUS agreement was formed out of a concern that China is a real threat to Australia. But this is concerning as many who addressed the commissioners pointed out that this risk wasn’t there.

We need to know where the intelligence that China is a “threat” is coming from.

China is one of our biggest trading partners, and Australians need to know whether there is a threat.

Former defence minister Linda Reynolds said that Australia was already under threat from China. This was worrying and concerning. But we don’t know how real that threat is.

There is a real concern that the AUKUS agreement is taking us towards a conflict, with the US dictating.

There are still a lot of unknowns around how the AUKUS agreement is going to roll out across Australia.

Australia has already invested billions into the British and US submarine building shipyards. Taxpayers should be concerned that these nuclear-powered submarines could potentially be managed and controlled by the US on Australian soil.

Australians need to be asking their local members of parliament questions around what AUKUS is getting us into.

We created a space with this AUKUS public inquiry to hear the voices of Australians as our own government didn’t allow us to have a say. They did not run a parliamentary inquiry.

AUKUS is a concern for all Australians. It is not just a First Nations issue because of the radioactive waste problem. It is local communities that are going to be impacted if US bases are going to be put on local soil.

[This slightly abridged piece was first published by Sydney Criminal Lawyers, for which Paul Gregoire writes.]
